3. In a royal context, it is the scepter, the visible insignia of the power and legitimacy of the king, marking his right to govern.
H7626H.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to divide" or "to share." It first designates a branch or stem — that which divides and multiplies. This image of the rod representing a branch of the genealogical tree has naturally led to the meaning "tribe": like a branch, each tribe is a division of the people, stemming from the same root. The rod becomes the visible symbol of this authority and continuity.
H7626H.emploi: The word appears 125 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Pentateuch and the historical books. It almost always designates the twelve tribes of Israel or one of them in particular. It is encountered when speaking of the inheritance of lands (Joshua 13:14), the census of the people (2 Samuel 24:2), the revelation of the Law to the assembly of the tribes (Deuteronomy 5:23), or the recognition of the leaders of each tribe (Deuteronomy 1:13-15). Sometimes, the meaning shifts toward symbolism: the tribe can evoke the authority that a leader exercises over his group, or the scepter as a mark of that power.
H7626H.portee: Understanding the tribe helps the reader grasp how God constituted Israel: not as a disorganized crowd, but as a people structured into extended families, each bearing its history and place in the divine plan. This reveals that God honors order, genealogical continuity, and group solidarity. For the Christian, this illustrates how God chooses an organized people and how each belongs to a community with shared responsibilities.

sens: Throwing weapon: a pointed shaft thrown by hand
Stick, rod, or rigid wooden shaft
Mark of authority: scepter or insignia of royal power
Group of related families: tribe or clan
H7626I.detail:
1. The javelin is a weapon of war that the soldier holds in hand and throws against the enemy. Joab uses it to kill Absalom, who is caught hanging from an oak tree (2 Samuel 18:14).
2. The word also refers to a simple stick or rod, a straight and hard wooden staff: this is the basic image of the word.
3. In the case of a king or leader, the scepter (staff of authority) bears this name because it symbolizes power and command, like the shepherd's staff that governs his flock.
4. A tribe or clan is called this because it forms a united, solid group, distinct from others, like the branches of the same family: each tribe of Israel descends from a son of Jacob.
H7626I.origine: The Hebrew word שֵׁבֶט comes from a root that evokes the idea of striking or leading. The basic image is that of a straight and rigid shaft: staff, rod, branch. From this arise all the meanings: the shepherd's rod, the king's scepter, the warrior's weapon, and the human group united like a solid shaft. The word often appears with the meaning of tribe in the Old Testament.
H7626I.emploi: This Hebrew word has several uses depending on the context. In 2 Samuel 18:14, it clearly refers to the javelin, the pointed weapon that Joab thrusts into the heart of Absalom. Elsewhere in the Bible, it carries other meanings: the shepherd's staff (like that of Moses or Aaron), the scepter of the king or judge, or the group of the twelve tribes of Israel (with Joseph sometimes forming two half-tribes). Thus, the same word carries several related meanings that all revolve around the idea of a shaft, power, or unity.
H7626I.portee: This word reminds us that in Israel, power and authority find their expression in a concrete object: the scepter, the judge's staff, the prophet's rod. It is also the word that unites the twelve tribes into a people chosen by God. For the believer, it evokes how God governs His people through His representatives and how a united community forms the strength of a nation.

sens: Division of the people of Israel, each descending from one of the twelve sons of Jacob
Human group sharing a common origin and a common leader
Group of people forming a supportive community
H7626J.detail:
1. A tribe is primarily a division of the people of Israel: each of the twelve major families descending from the twelve sons of Jacob. It is the basic political and social organization of God's people. In 2 Samuel 7:7, God tells David that He has walked with Israel and has not commanded any of the tribes regarding the construction of a temple: each tribe represents a part of the whole people.
2. A tribe more broadly designates a human group united by a common ancestry and led by a chief or ancestor. It is a natural community, where the bonds of kinship and loyalty are strong.
3. The word extends to any group of people forming a solid and organized unit, whether they are linked by blood or by covenant.
H7626J.origine: The Hebrew word שׁבט (shebet) comes from a root evoking the idea of striking or dividing. Its primary meaning is "staff" or "rod," symbolizing the power of the leader or shepherd. From this derives the meaning of "tribe": the shepherd's rod that leads the flock, or the king's scepter that governs. The same root also produces "scepter," the insignia of authority. A tribe is therefore primarily a group guided by a leader who bears this insignia.
H7626J.emploi: The word appears in the Greek New Testament (phulè) to designate the twelve tribes of Israel. In the provided usage (2 Samuel 7:7), God speaks of the tribes as divisions of the people to whom He has given shepherds: each tribe is a distinct entity that God recognizes and governs. The term is also used to refer to the twelve tribes as a whole, as historical and religious entities of the covenant people.
H7626J.portee: Understanding that God organized His people into tribes reminds us that the Church is a body composed of many members. Each tribe had its role, its heritage, its place in the divine plan. This invites us to see our own Christian community not as a shapeless mass, but as a structured people where each has an identity and a responsibility.

sens: Eleventh month of the post-exilic Jewish calendar
H7627.detail: Schebat is the name of the eleventh month of the Hebrew calendar as it was established after the Babylonian exile. It corresponds to the period of late January or early February in our current calendar. It is during this month, on the 24th of Schebat in the second year of King Darius of Persia, that the prophet Zechariah received a word from the Lord.
H7627.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "staff" or "rod." The eleventh month bears this name due to an ancient association, perhaps linked to the winter period or to Babylonian calendrical practices that the Jews adopted during their exile. After the return from exile, this twelve-month lunar calendar became established in Jewish practice.
H7627.emploi: Schebat appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 1:7. The prophet dates his vision to the 24th of Schebat, indicating that this month was already well established in the official dating of events during the post-exilic period of the prophet Zechariah. This precise detail of the date highlights the importance of situating prophetic words within a recognized historical and calendrical framework.
H7627.portee: This mention reminds us that the word of God intervenes in concrete human history, dated and locatable. It also teaches us how, upon returning from exile, the Jewish people reorganized themselves with their own civil and religious structures, including their calendar.

sens: State of one who is a prisoner, detained or enslaved
Action of capturing, of making a prisoner
Group of people taken prisoner or deported
Forced deportation of a people from their land
H7628A.detail:
1. Captivity is primarily the state of one who is held forcibly, reduced to helplessness. A captive is a prisoner, as clearly stated in Exodus 12:29 by mentioning "the captive in his prison." It is the condition of someone who has lost their freedom.
2. The word also designates the act of capturing: taking someone, making them a prisoner. Numbers 21:1 and 31:12 speak of those who are "taken captive" during battles.
3. Captivity can also refer to the group of captives themselves, those who have been seized. Ezra 8:35 calls the exiles returned from Babylon "sons of the captivity," marking that these people form a collective.
4. In the history of Israel, the word especially evokes the forced deportation of a people from their promised land. Jeremiah 30:10 promises deliverance: "I will deliver you from the distant land; I will deliver your offspring from the land where they are captive." It is the political and spiritual exile, the ultimate punishment.
H7628A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to take" or "to seize." It concretely expresses the action of capturing in battle: seizing an enemy, holding them. The family of this word includes terms designating the taking of spoils, the prisoner, the prey. In biblical Hebrew, the word applies equally to the capture of an individual and to the mass deportation of a nation.
H7628A.emploi: The word appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Ezra, Nehemiah, Chronicles) and prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). In the war narratives (Numbers 21, 31; Deuteronomy 21), it names the prisoners or the human spoils. It takes on major theological significance in the context of the Babylonian exile: Ezra and Nehemiah refer to the returned exiles as "sons of the captivity," recognizing this moment as defining. In Jeremiah and Ezekiel, the prophets announce the exile or promise liberation — the word becomes key to understanding God's judgment and His mercy. Psalm 68:19 metaphorizes it: God "takes captivity captive," meaning He frees the prisoners.
H7628A.portee: For the Christian reader, the word captivity reminds us that man can be held in slavery — not only in a political or military sense but also spiritually. The Bible shows that Israel experienced captivity as a consequence of unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:41), but also that God promises deliverance and restoration (Jeremiah 30:10). This word becomes a figure of spiritual liberation: one who understands that sin makes one "captive" will find true freedom in salvation.

sens: Person made prisoner in war or reduced to slavery
State of one who is deprived of freedom
H7628B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a person taken in war and brought into captivity: Barak must bring his captives after the victory (Judges 5:12). This refers to a prisoner of war, stripped of their freedom and often destined for slavery or servitude.
2. Figuratively, it also describes the state of enslavement, the deprivation of freedom: Jerusalem itself is called "Captive, daughter of Zion" (Isaiah 52:2) to signify its state of oppression and submission under the enemy's yoke.
H7628B.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁבִי (shvi) comes from the root שׁבה (shbh), meaning "to take captive," "to lead into captivity." This root evokes the action of seizing and leading someone away from their home, from their freedom. Biblical texts use this word and its family to describe both the act of capture and the resulting state: being captive, living in captivity.
H7628B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. In Judges 5:12, it refers to the prisoners of war that Barak must bring back after his victory over Sisera — a concrete and historical usage. In Isaiah 52:2, it takes on a symbolic meaning: Jerusalem itself is addressed as a captive, expressing its enslavement to a foreign power and the expectation of its deliverance. These two usages show how a word describing a prisoner can become an image of the oppression of an entire people.
H7628B.portee: This word reminds Israel and the reader that captivity is a terrible reality, but never a definitive one. The call to captive Jerusalem (Isaiah 52) announces an imminent liberation: God will not leave His people in chains forever. For the Christian, this also speaks of the bondage of sin and the freedom that only God can provide.

sens: Son of Nachash, Ammonite prince during the time of the united monarchy
H7629.detail: Schobi is an Ammonite prince, son of King Nachash of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. He appears only once in the Bible, during Absalom's revolt against his father David. As David flees Jerusalem, Schobi and other notable figures (Makir and Barzillai) go to Mahanaim to bring provisions, beds, and utensils to the king and his court — a valuable aid in a time of crisis (2 Samuel 17:27-29). This gesture shows that even foreign leaders recognized David as a legitimate king worthy of support.
H7629.origine: The name Schobi means "glorious" in Hebrew, formed from a root that evokes splendor and honor. It is a royal name, fitting for one who is the son of an Ammonite king.
H7629.emploi: Schobi appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 17:27. He is among the local supporters that David receives at the critical moment when he must flee from the revolt of his son Absalom. His intervention shows that David's prestige extended beyond the borders of Israel and that foreign princes saw him as a valuable ally.
H7629.portee: The example of Schobi reminds us that God can raise support for His servants from unexpected sources. Even an Ammonite prince, from a nation often hostile to Israel, recognizes the dignity and authority of David in his misfortune. This serves as encouragement to trust in divine providence during trials.

sens: Ancestor of a family of temple porters
Head of a family who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H7630.detail: Schobaï is the name of a man who lived during the time of exile and return. He is mentioned as the ancestor of a family of temple porters (Ezra 2:42). His name means "glorious" in Hebrew, which was fitting for one who guarded the entrance to the house of God. After the captivity in Babylon, his family was among the exiles who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple. The descendants of Schobaï, numbering one hundred thirty-nine according to Ezra and one hundred thirty-eight according to Nehemiah, resumed their duties as guardians of the sanctuary, an important role in the restored worship.
H7630.origine: The name Schobaï comes from Hebrew and means "glorious." This name carries the idea of splendor and dignity, qualities appropriate for one who guarded access to the temple, the holiest place in Israel.
H7630.emploi: Schobaï is mentioned twice in the Bible, each time in the context of the return from exile. He appears in Ezra 2:42 and Nehemiah 7:45, two passages that list the families who returned from captivity. In both cases, his family is identified as that of the temple porters, responsible for guarding the gates of the sanctuary. The numbers vary slightly between the two lists (one hundred thirty-nine in Ezra, one hundred thirty-eight in Nehemiah), but the role remains the same: these men served God by ensuring the guardianship of the rebuilt temple.

sens: Fire that bursts forth from a source of heat or combustion
Luminous and mobile aspect of fire
Image of divine power and majesty
H7631.detail:
1. The word designates the visible fire that burns, bursts forth, and consumes. In Daniel 3:22, the flame of the extraordinarily heated furnace kills the king's soldiers who get too close — it refers to the intense heat and active, devastating fire.
2. The flame also evokes the luminous aspect of fire, its dance and mobility. It is the movement of fire, its characteristic flickering: in Daniel 7:9, the prophet sees God's throne as flames of fire, an image of liveliness and power in motion.
3. In this divine context, the flame becomes an image of God's power, majesty, and holiness. It is no longer just material fire, but the symbol of the glory and absolute authority of the Ancient of Days.
H7631.origine: The Aramaic word שְׂבִיב (seviv) likely has its root in the Hebrew word שָׁבִיב (shaviv), which also means "flame" and comes from a root evoking the circular and rapid movement of fire. The dancing and swirling fire is captured in this image. The same family designates the bursting forth, the energy of fire in action.
H7631.emploi: The word appears twice in Daniel, both in key passages where fire plays a theological role. In Daniel 3:22, it refers to the material, destructive fire that protects the three young men but kills their persecutors: the flame executes judgment. In Daniel 7:9, the grand vision of the eternal God uses the image of flames to describe the divine throne — here the flame expresses holiness, irrepressible energy, and the transcendent majesty of divine judgment. The word thus transitions from the concrete to the symbolic and theological.
H7631.portee: The flame reminds the reader that God is not an abstract or tranquil power: He is a living holiness, an active will, capable of protecting His servants and judging His enemies. The image of the flaming throne invites reverence and certainty that God's judgment is real and irrevocable. It calls the believer not to fear earthly persecutors, for God remains the absolute sovereign.

sens: A jet of fire that rises from a hearth or a source of combustion
Figuratively: brilliance, liveliness, that which shines and radiates
H7632.detail: 1. A flame is the fire that bursts forth and rises from a burning hearth — what one sees when looking at the embers of a fire. In Job 18:5, it speaks of "the flame that bursts forth" from the wicked, as if their light and brilliance – their prestige, their apparent success – rise from them, but ultimately extinguish. 2. Figuratively, the flame denotes anything that shines, anything that radiates and attracts attention: the brilliance of a prosperous life, the liveliness of one who seems to flourish. The psalmist uses this image to show that the brightness of the wicked is only temporary, ephemeral like a flame that goes out.
H7632.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁבִיב comes from a root that means "to burn" or "to shine intensely." It describes the concrete image of fire that rises and sparkles. The Aramaic has a very similar word, שְׂבִיב, with the same meaning of flame. The word evokes the visual and luminous impression of fire — that which rises, that which illuminates, that which fascinates by its movement.
H7632.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 18:5. It is found in the speech of Bildad, who paints the inevitable fate of the wicked: their light will go out, and the flame (their brilliance, their apparent prosperity) will cease to shine. This passage uses the image of fire going out to express the idea that the prosperity of the wicked is temporary and fragile, like a flame that is blown out.
H7632.portee: This image of the flame that goes out speaks to the believer about the fragility of everything that shines without God. It invites us not to admire or envy the deceptive brilliance of the success of the wicked, but to understand that only the light that comes from God lasts forever. It is a call to seek a brilliance that does not extinguish.

sens: a person captured in war, taken prisoner
the state of captivity, slavery
the collective of captives, prisoners taken in war
H7633.detail:
1. A captive is a person taken in war, torn from their freedom and homeland. In Deuteronomy 21:11, the text speaks of a beautiful woman seen among the "captives" — women forcibly taken by victorious warriors. It is the image of the defeated stripped of all autonomy.
2. The word also designates the very state of captivity, the condition of enslavement. In Nehemiah 4:4, prayer is made against those who want to bring Israel back into captivity — it is the situation of loss of freedom that threatens.
3. Used in the plural, "captives" or "captive women" groups all the prisoners from a single capture, as in 2 Chronicles 28:11 where it calls to send back "these captives you have taken among your brothers" — a human crowd torn from their loved ones.
H7633.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of capturing, of trapping. It is a noun that first designates the state (captivity, what you endure), then the person who experiences it (the captive). The same root appears in other terms related to war and enslavement.
H7633.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly in passages of war and exile. It is especially found in 2 Chronicles 28, where King Ahaz suffers a defeat, and the Syrians and the Northern Israelites capture thousands of his subjects. The text emphasizes the moral obligation to send back the "captives" — showing that even war has limits and that one cannot enslave their brothers. In Deuteronomy 21:11 and 32:42, it is encountered in the code of war and in the vision of divine judgment. The word balances between two meanings: the captive person and the state of captivity in which they live.
H7633.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that captivity is real — it can be physical, but also spiritual: slaves to sin, to lies, to shame. Yet the Bible proclaims that God frees the captives: this is a major theme that the prophets will reiterate. Understanding that one was "captive" helps to measure the grace of deliverance and to foster gratitude towards the one who sets us free.

sens: Benjaminite from the time of the divided monarchy, son of Shaharaim
H7634.detail: Shocja is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, living at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. He was the son of Shaharaim and Hodesh, and one of several children listed in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:10). His name appears in this genealogical context as a family head among the descendants of Benjamin.
H7634.origine: The name Shocja literally means "announcement" or "proclamation." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of making known or proclaiming. Like many Hebrew names in the Old Testament, it reflects a word or an event of spiritual significance at the time of birth.
H7634.emploi: Shocja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:10, where he is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is listed among the sons of Shaharaim and Hodesh, alongside his brothers Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuts, Mirma, Abitub, and Elpaal. The Bible explicitly designates him as a family head, indicating that he played a role of responsibility and authority in his lineage.

sens: A narrow way or road that one walks on foot
A spiritual or moral path that one follows
H7635.detail:
1. The path is a marked way, generally narrow, that one travels on foot. In Psalms 77:20, the Lord "makes a way through the sea": He creates a path, a road through the waters, where ordinarily there is none. It is the image of a passage made possible, a way opened in the midst of an obstacle.
2. Figuratively, the path also denotes a way of life, a spiritual direction one adopts. In Jeremiah 18:15, the people have "forsaken the ancient paths" to follow unmarked ways: it is abandoning the right way of God to stray into idolatry. The path then becomes an image of faithfulness or spiritual wandering.
H7635.origine: The Hebrew word šəbûl literally means "that which is trodden" or "that which is beaten"—a path that is regularly traveled until the ground is worn. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of treading, of walking along. This image of the path trodden by footsteps evokes both the practicability and the wear of time: a true path is one that many have traveled.
H7635.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Psalms 77:20, it describes the miraculous path that God creates through the sea—a way that is impossible made possible by His intervention. In Jeremiah 18:15, it stands in contrast to "unmarked ways": the ancient paths are those of divine tradition and faithfulness, while the new paths that the people follow are diverted, unholy ways. The word emphasizes the idea of an established and recognized direction.
H7635.portee: The path speaks to the believer of two realities: first, that God opens paths, that He creates a way even where it seems impossible; secondly, that faith consists in staying on the ancient paths, the ways established by God and His prophets, rather than being led astray to new and deceptive paths. It is a powerful image of faithfulness and trust in divine guidance.

sens: band or ornament worn around the forehead or head
luxurious female accessory in antiquity
H7636.detail:
1. A headband is a narrow strip or band, often decorated, that women wore around their forehead or head as an ornament. It is a type of diadem or precious band. In Isaiah 3:18, the prophet lists the luxurious adornments that the women of Jerusalem will lose in judgment: the Lord will remove the "headbands," the anklets on their feet, the crescents, and other beautiful items — all signs of vanity and wealth.
2. This ornament also carries a moral and spiritual meaning: it represents the pride of women attached to appearance and seduction rather than to the true inner beauty that Scripture values.
H7636.origine: The Hebrew word shabîs specifically refers to a band or headband wrapped around the head. Its basic image is that of a tie or strip. In the biblical context, it is a typically female accessory of a certain social rank, in line with the customs of the ancient Near East where wealthy women wore diadems, headbands, and ornamental veils.
H7636.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 3:18. The prophet enumerates a long list of ornaments and adornments that the arrogant women of Jerusalem wore with pride — headbands, anklets, chains, pendants, bracelets, veils — all signs of worldly vanity. This accumulation of luxurious items underscores God's judgment against superficial pride: all these beautiful things will disappear. The headband here is a symbol of wealth and carnal seduction.
H7636.portee: This passage reminds us that God looks at the heart far more than at outward appearance. The accumulation of expensive ornaments means nothing in the face of God's judgment on pride and vanity. For the Christian, this text invites us to seek true beauty, that of the soul and spirit, rather than placing our assurance in material wealth and transient adornments.

sens: The number seven, in ordinal position, that comes after the sixth
The day of the week dedicated to rest, the Sabbath
The day or month marking a sacred cycle or an important religious feast
What completes or finishes a cycle of seven elements
A repetition or waiting for the seventh day
H7637.detail:
1. It is simply the number seven in terms of rank: the seventh day comes after six other days, the seventh month after six other months (Exodus 24:16: "On the seventh day, the Lord called to Moses from the midst of the cloud").
2. The weekly day of rest, dedicated to God and inactivity (Exodus 20:10: "You shall do no work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant" — it is the seventh day that is being referred to).
3. A day or month marked by a feast, a holy convocation, or a solemn religious obligation: the Feast of Unleavened Bread ends on the seventh day (Leviticus 23:8: "On the seventh day, there shall be a holy convocation"), or the seventh month hosts several important feasts (Numbers 29:1).
4. In a cycle of seven occurrences (seven days of marching around Jericho, Joshua 6:4-16), the seventh completes and realizes what has been promised or initiated.
5. A duration of waiting or separation: leprosy must be examined on the seventh day to verify its healing (Leviticus 13:5), or servitude lasts six years before freedom on the seventh (Exodus 21:2).
H7637.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "sheba" (שׁבע), which means "seven." The ordinal adjective "seventh" (שׁבִיעִי) gives the number seven its rank function in a sequence. The number seven carries a profound religious significance throughout the Bible: it represents fullness, perfection, the completion of a cycle in the presence of God. This is why the seventh day is blessed and consecrated (Genesis 2:2-3), and why events marked by the seal of seven — seventh day, seventh year, seventh time — are always moments filled with divine meaning.
H7637.emploi: The word appears 94 times in the Bible, almost always in reference to a specific day or month. It is particularly dense in the books of the Law: Exodus (about 35 occurrences), Leviticus (about 30), and Numbers (about 15). The contexts vary: the seventh day of creation and rest (Genesis 2:2-3), the prohibition of work on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10), religious feasts set on the seventh day or seventh month (Leviticus 23), cycles of purification or observation (Leviticus 13-14), the release of Hebrew slaves every seven years (Exodus 21:2), and specific military or political events such as the siege of Jericho (Joshua 6). The meaning remains constant: it always marks a completion, a sacredness, or a significant break in time.
H7637.portee: For the believer, the seventh day reminds us that God Himself rested from His works and sanctified this day (Genesis 2:3). It is a sign of covenant: observing the rest of the seventh day is to acknowledge that the world belongs to God and that man should not dominate through incessant labor. The number seven and its cycles also mark the structure of divine grace: religious feasts, jubilee years, and God's redemptive acts follow this rhythm. This speaks to the heart of the Christian about the importance of rest in God and the trust placed in Him, far from incessant work.

sens: Openwork structure made of crossed threads or rods in diamonds or squares
Ornament in the form of a network on a capital or architectural structure
Net or trap woven to catch animals
H7639.detail:
1. The lattice is primarily a structure made of interwoven materials — such as threads, ropes, or rods — that form a pattern of diamonds or regular meshes. One can see through it, but the elements stop passage. In the architecture of Solomon's Temple, bronze lattices adorn the capitals of the columns, decorated with pomegranates: it is both an artistic and structural motif (1 Kings 7:17).
2. This ornamental network motif adorns the tops of the columns of the Temple, arranged in festoons or shaped chains. It is a prestigious trim that crowns the bronze columns and frames the pomegranates (1 Kings 7:20).
3. Figuratively, the lattice also refers to a trap or net for capturing animals — a structure that encloses and holds, just as the crossed network captures anyone who ventures into it (Job 18:8).
H7639.origine: The word comes from the root שׂבַךְ (savakh), which means "to intertwine" or "to weave together." This root evokes the action of crossing and intertwining elements to make a coherent whole. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms describing woven or knotted structures — works that require craftsmanship and precision.
H7639.emploi: The word appears about twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the description of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 7 and parallels in 2 Chronicles 4) and in the account of the destruction of the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52). It then designates the bronze lattices that adorn the capitals of the two great columns of the Temple, called Jakin and Boaz. The context repeats the image of the pomegranates arranged around these lattices — a detail of wealth and splendor. The word also appears once in the metaphorical sense of a trap or net that captures (Job 18:8), always remaining linked to the idea of a crossing structure that holds or encloses.
H7639.portee: The lattice of the Temple recalls the wisdom and wealth of Solomon: every detail of the divine edifice reflects an elaborate and thoughtful beauty. For the believer, the image of the lattice as a trap in Job invites vigilance — we can be captured by the traps of sin and temptation, and that is why the Word calls us to remain watchful.

sens: Floating and ample part of a garment that trails or extends to the ground
Lower edge of a garment, especially a dress or tunic
Image of wealth, dignity, personal ornamentation
H7640.detail:
1. The word refers to the portion of the garment that hangs freely from the waist or hips, floating around the body. In Isaiah 47:2, it speaks of the "hem" of the dress that the young woman must "lift" (that is, tuck up) to cross the rivers: this gesture shows how these hems can hinder walking, dragging on the ground or in the water. It is a garment of considerable fullness, that of a free and affluent woman.
2. Figuratively, the hem of a garment symbolizes the elegance, grace, or wealth of the wearer. In the context of Isaiah 47, lifting her hems is an act of humiliation: the woman who was to be splendid becomes servile and exposed, stripped of her dignity.
H7640.origine: The Hebrew word sho.vel likely comes from a root meaning that which extends, floats, or hangs. In Hebrew, loose garments, tunics, and richly adorned dresses are signs of high social status. The word evokes the concrete image of fabric that extends from the body, floating and visible to all, making it a key element of the distinctive appearance of high-ranking women.
H7640.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 47:2. In this prophetic passage, the prophet addresses the daughter of Babylon, commanding her to lift the hems of her dress to cross the rivers. This injunction expresses the humiliation and fall of Babylon: she who was adorned and majestic must strip away her splendor and act like a servant. The word is thus used to remind of a dramatic contrast between past dignity and the impending humiliation.
H7640.portee: This word invites reflection on the vanity of outward signs of power and wealth. Babylon, proud in her splendor, must abandon her ornaments: she understands that beauty and elegance of clothing do not protect against God's judgment. For the believer, this reminds us that true dignity does not reside in adornment or status, but in the fear of the Lord.

sens: To cover with a large amount of water
To completely submerge
Figuratively: to overwhelm, crush under the weight of
H7641A.detail:
1. The word literally describes the action of water rising and covering: in Psalm 69:3, the psalmist says "the waters flood me," comparing his distress to a tide that submerges him. It is the image of a flood, an overflow that invades everything.
2. Strictly speaking, to flood means to be submerged, carried away by the waters — like someone sinking into the water and unable to breathe. The image is one of imminent drowning, of losing control in the face of a greater force.
3. But the Bible also uses this word figuratively to express moral overwhelm: the psalmist is not speaking of a real flood, but of his soul crushed by suffering. The "waters" that flood him are actually his misfortunes, his pains, his troubles that overwhelm him like waves (Psalms 69:16).
H7641A.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁבּוֹלֶת comes from a root evoking flowing water, a current. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting running water, stream, current. The basic image is that of the movement of water, its overflowing flow. It is not still water, but water that moves with force.
H7641A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Psalm 69, where it denotes the experience of the psalmist overwhelmed by misfortune. In verse 3, he cries: "the waters flood me" — he sinks into the mud, fallen into an aquatic pit. In verse 16, he repeats: "let not the waters that flood me engulf me." It is a prayer not to be entirely submerged, engulfed. The context is always one of distress, imminent danger, fear of being crushed. The Bible uses this word to express not a concrete flood, but a moral and spiritual trial experienced as drowning.
H7641A.portee: This word helps the reader understand the depth of suffering expressed in the Psalms. When we say that the waters flood us, we are speaking of something stronger than ourselves, a trial that overwhelms and submerges us. For the suffering Christian, this biblical language shows that God understands and even welcomes the raw expression of despair — and that prayer consists of crying out to God precisely in that moment when one feels drowned.

sens: Head of ripe or growing grain, borne by the stalk of wheat or barley
Cluster of grains grouped at the top of a cereal plant
What the reaper cuts and gathers
Figuratively: the years or resources represented by the ears
H7641B.detail:
1. The ear is the upper part of the grain stalk where the grains develop. In Genesis 41:5, Pharaoh sees "seven fat and beautiful ears" rising on a single stalk — it is the image of healthy wheat that has grown well, the grains are full and heavy.
2. Several ears or clusters of grains form the entirety of the harvest. In Ruth 2:2, Ruth asks to "glean ears" in the field: she gathers the ears forgotten by the reapers, the bundles of grains left after the harvest.
3. During the harvest, the reaper "cuts the ears" with his sickle or arm (Isaiah 17:5). It is the concrete work: cutting the stalks laden with grain and gathering them.
4. In Pharaoh's dream, the ears no longer represent just physical grain: the seven fat ears signify seven years of abundance, and the seven thin ears signify seven years of famine (Genesis 41:26-27). The word becomes the image of time passing and what it brings.
H7641B.origine: The Hebrew word shib'boleth (שִׁבֹּ֫לֶת) derives from a root meaning growth and flourishing. It concretely designates the head or ear of grain in the process of maturation. The same word, with the meaning of "flow" or "current," can also mean a torrent or watercourse, an image born from the fluidity of ears that undulate like a wave. The word is regularly attested in biblical Hebrew in the context of harvests and prophetic dreams.
H7641B.emploi: The word "ear" (shib'boleth) appears 12 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Genesis 41 (Pharaoh's dream), where it describes the visions of seven years of abundance and famine. It is also found in Ruth 2 (Ruth gleaning in Boaz's field), where it refers to the remaining ears to be harvested. In Isaiah 17:5, the prophet uses the image of the reaper cutting the ears to evoke the ruin of a people. In Job 24:24, we see the ear "bowing down" and disappearing, an image of fragility. Each usage is situated in the concrete (the harvest, famine) or in the figurative (the passage of time, destruction), but the image remains that of ripe grain, rich in meaning according to the context.
H7641B.portee: The ear speaks to us of natural cycles and providence. Pharaoh's dream reminds us that God controls time, seasons, abundance, and scarcity. The image of Ruth gleaning the ears evokes God's mercy toward the weak and the foreigner. For the Christian, the ear also reminds us that we reap what we have sown, and that our lives are part of a divine plan of which we see only fragments.

sens: Arm or course of a river
Flow or current of water
Region traversed by a watercourse
H7641G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the ear or the ear of grain — the image of a stem that bends and flows. Applied to water, it evokes the flow that runs like the bent grains: it is the current of a river, its course. In Isaiah 27:12, "from the course of the river to the torrent of Egypt" describes the boundaries of the territory of Israel from north to south, along these waterways.
2. By extension, the word can designate any portion of water that flows, not just the Nile or the Euphrates: it is a fluid way of speaking about the movement of waters.
3. Figuratively, the "course" becomes the region itself, defined by the river that traverses it — the territory that is bathed and delineated by moving water.
H7641G.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁבֹּלֶת comes from a root that evokes the idea of flowing or bending — like the ears of grain that bend and sway in the wind. The primary image is therefore that of something that flows, that streams. Applied to water, it is naturally the current of a river. The same word appears in the book of Judges (12:6) as a term of recognition ("shiboleth" in transliterated French), where it becomes the word of a people — a powerful image of the flow that separates those who pronounce it.
H7641G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in this sense: in Isaiah 27:12, where the prophet describes how God will beat the fruits of the world like one shakes the ear, and he uses "course" to geographically situate the action. It is a poetic way of designating the great riverways — the Euphrates in the north and the torrent of Egypt in the south — that mark the borders of the promised territory to Israel. The term remains rare and its use is very localized in the prophetic books.
H7641G.portee: This word reminds us that God masters the waters and the territories: He "shakes" them like one shakes the ears, to gather the fruit. For the believer, it is an image of the final harvest, where God gathers His scattered people from one end of the earth to the other, from the most distant rivers to the borders He has drawn.

sens: Ear of grain in formation
Small stream that flows
Signal of recognition or password
H7641H.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word designates the ear or the emerging ear of grain, especially of barley or wheat — the part of the plant that bears the grains. In Judges 12:6, the word "Shibboleth" is used as a test: the Gileadites asked the fugitives from Samaria to pronounce this word to identify them, as the pronunciation varied from region to region.
2. The word can also designate a small stream or brook that flows — an image drawn from the movement of grain that sways in the wind or of water that flows. This natural and fluid image gives the word its double resonance: something that grows and flows.
3. Metaphorically, the word has become a signal of identification or a password: something that reveals belonging to a group, as only those who speak the local dialect pronounce it correctly. It is a test that distinguishes friends from enemies.
H7641H.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of growth and flow. The basic image is that of the ear growing on the stem, or of the brook flowing — two natural movements. In Hebrew, the same root appears in other words related to water and vegetation. The word has retained its concrete meaning while acquiring a symbolic significance of recognition and distinction between peoples.
H7641H.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Judges 12:6, in the episode of the war between the Gileadites and the Ephraimites. After the military victory, the Gileadites stationed guards at the fords of the Jordan to stop the fugitives. They used the word "Shibboleth" as a test: the Ephraimites, whose dialect pronounced this word differently, could not say it correctly, which betrayed them. This unique use of the word makes it historically and culturally significant, as it illustrates how a simple word can serve to identify a distinct group.
H7641H.portee: This passage shows us how differences in language and culture reveal our origins and affiliations. For the Christian, it invites reflection on what truly identifies us: not our ability to pronounce the right words, but our heart and our faith. It is a reminder that God sees beyond appearances and human recognition codes.

sens: Small mollusk with a spiral shell
Figuratively, that which melts away and disappears
H7642.detail:
1. The snail is a small creeping animal protected by a spiral shell. In Psalms 58:9, the psalmist uses the image of the snail that melts — probably referring to the slimy trail it leaves behind — to describe something that gradually disappears, that consumes itself. It is an insignificant and fragile creature.
2. The text applies this image to the dissolution of the wicked: "Let them perish as they melt away, like a snail." The snail symbolizes here the slow disappearance, the gradual collapse of one who opposes God, an end without glory and without trace.
H7642.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the slow and sliding movement of this creature. The snail was known in the Eastern Mediterranean and in ancient Near East as an animal of wet grounds. The image was striking for a Middle Eastern audience: the snail, as it moves, leaves behind a trail of slime and seems to melt into the ground.
H7642.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 58:9. The psalmist makes it a symbol of the fate of God's enemies: they will melt away and disappear like this insignificant creature. The context is a psalm of supplication where the author asks God to punish those who commit iniquity. The snail represents less an animal than an image of dissolution and disappearance.
H7642.portee: This image of the melting snail speaks to us of the fragility of those who oppose God. It assures the believer that evil will not endure, that God's enemies — however powerful they may seem — will ultimately consume themselves and disappear without a trace. It is a promise of hope for those who suffer from injustice.

sens: City of Moab east of the Jordan
H7643G.detail: Sebam is a city located in Moab, in the pastoral region east of the Jordan. It is among the cities that the tribes of Reuben and Gad ask Moses to assign to them as an inheritance during the conquest of the land (Numbers 32:3). Its name, according to tradition, would mean "fragrance" or "perfume."
H7643G.origine: The name Sebam (also known in the forms Shibmah or Sibmah) would mean "fragrance" or "perfume," perhaps evoking the agricultural richness or aromatic plants of this region of Moab. The Semitic origin of the name reflects its identity as a city of the highlands east of the Jordan.
H7643G.emploi: Sebam appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 32:3, where it is mentioned by the representatives of the tribes of Reuben and Gad who list the cities of the Moabite territory they wish to occupy and cultivate after the conquest of the land. This mention clearly situates Sebam in the context of the distribution of lands among the tribes of Israel.

sens: Moabite city east of the Jordan
region of renowned vineyards
H7643H.detail:
1. Sibma is a city located in Moab, east of the Jordan, which initially belonged to the Amorites before being assigned to the tribes of Reuben and Gad (Numbers 32:38). It also appears in the list of cities of Judah according to Joshua 13:19.
2. Sibma is especially famous for its exceptional vineyards, whose branches spread widely across the region, even beyond the sea (Isaiah 16:8). This fertility and abundance make Sibma a symbol of prosperity in the prophecies against Moab (Jeremiah 48:32).
H7643H.origine: The name Sibma means "fragrance," suggesting the pleasant scent of blooming vines and grapes. This name evokes the agricultural wealth and material blessing associated with this fertile region.
H7643H.emploi: Sibma appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always as a specific geographical location. It is first mentioned among the cities that Reuben and Gad built or renamed after conquering the Moabite territory (Numbers 32:38; Joshua 13:19). However, it is mainly in the prophecies against Moab, in Isaiah and Jeremiah, that Sibma returns as a symbol: its magnificent vineyards, which extended even beyond the sea, have become an object of prophetic lamentation (Isaiah 16:8-9; Jeremiah 48:32), as the region will be devastated during God's judgment on Moab.
H7643H.portee: Sibma teaches how material prosperity, even impressive, remains fragile before God's judgment. The renowned vineyards of Sibma also illustrate that divine blessing can manifest through earthly abundance, but this abundance never protects a nation that turns away from the Lord.

sens: High-ranking figure at the court of the kingdom of Judah
Secretary of King Hezekiah
Governor of the royal palace
H7644.detail: Schebna is a man who holds important positions in the administration of King Hezekiah of Judah during the siege of Jerusalem by the Assyrian army. He is first mentioned as "secretary" (or scribe) in negotiations with the envoys of the king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:18), alongside Eliakim and Joah. He is a trusted man of the royal palace, likely responsible for drafting official documents and managing diplomatic correspondence. The prophet Isaiah refers to him as "governor of the palace" (Isaiah 22:15), meaning he was responsible for the internal administration of the royal castle. Thus, Schebna represents the administrative and political elite of Jerusalem during this critical period.
H7644.origine: The Hebrew name שֶׁבְנָא (Schebna) means "vigor" or "strength," suggesting a man of energy and capability. His appearance in biblical texts is limited to the two centuries of the divided monarchy. He embodies the type of high-ranking official in the ancient Near Eastern kingdoms.
H7644.emploi: Schebna appears nine times in the Bible, mainly in the accounts of the siege of Sennacherib and in the book of Isaiah. In 2 Kings (18-19), he is presented as the king's secretary during negotiations with the Assyrian envoys; he accompanies Eliakim to the prophet Isaiah to request his intercession. In the book of Isaiah (chapters 22 and 36-37), he bears the title of "governor of the palace" and is among the high dignitaries of the court. These passages show Schebna as a figure of real political importance, involved in major decisions of the kingdom in the face of foreign threat.
H7644.portee: The mention of Schebna illustrates how God acts through political events and the characters in place, even ordinary officials of the administration. His story reminds us that government officials, great or small, remain under God's watch and can be instruments of His will or witnesses to His acts.

sens: Musical priest serving in David's Temple
H7645G.detail: Schebania is a Levitical priest who lived during the time of David, king of Israel. His name means "increased by the Lord." He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 15:24 as one of the priests responsible for sounding the trumpets before the ark of God during its transfer to Jerusalem—a solemn ceremony of worship and praise. His role was therefore both religious and musical: producing the sounds that accompanied the worship of the people of Israel before the symbol of God's presence.
H7645G.origine: The name Schebania is formed from Hebrew roots meaning "Yah increases" or "the Lord increases." Similar names can be found in the Bible, notably Schebanyahu, which reflect the same divine blessing. This type of compound name, where the name of God (Yah) is added to a blessing or a verb, was common in Israel to express the covenant between God and His people.
H7645G.emploi: Schebania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:24. He was among the seven priests (or sacrificers) who assisted Obed-Edom and Jechijah as gatekeepers of the ark. His unique appearance in the account of the transport of the ark to Jerusalem indicates that he was one of the official religious figures of the Temple during David's reign. Although we know nothing else about his life, this single mention places him among the faithful servants of divine worship in Israel.

sens: Levite who participated in the spiritual restoration of Israel after the Babylonian exile
Spiritual leader involved in the renewed solemn covenant with God
H7645H.detail:
1. Schebania is a Levite mentioned during Israel's return from exile in Babylon, at the time of Nehemiah. He appears in Nehemiah 9:4 among those who ascended the platform of the Levites to cry out to the Lord during a great assembly of prayer and repentance.
2. He is also the one who, in Nehemiah 9:5, took part in the solemn exhortation to bless the Lord, confirming his role as a spiritual leader. In Nehemiah 10:10, his name appears among the leaders who sealed the renewed covenant with God, showing that he was one of the leaders of the restored community.
H7645H.origine: The name Schebania literally means "increased by Jehovah": it combines the idea of growth or increase with the divine name Jah (a shortened form of Jehovah). It is a typical name of the post-exilic period, reflecting confidence in divine blessing after the trial of captivity.
H7645H.emploi: Schebania is mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, all in chapters 9 and 10, during the restoration period after the return from exile (around the 5th century BCE). He appears in the context of national repentance and the renewal of the covenant: first as one of the Levites leading public prayer (Nehemiah 9:4-5), then as a signer of the covenant document (Nehemiah 10:10). His role is exclusively cultic and spiritual, participating in the reconstruction of Israel's religious life.
H7645H.portee: Schebania illustrates the essential role of the Levites in the spiritual restoration of Israel after the judgment of exile. His commitment to communal prayer and the renewed covenant shows how the faithful, even after captivity, can turn to God with sincerity and renew their commitment to Him. His example encourages Christians to recognize the importance of authentic spiritual leaders and collective repentance.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi or of the priestly class during the time of Nehemiah
H7645I.detail: Schebania is a character mentioned twice in the book of Nehemiah, during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. In Nehemiah 10:4, he appears among those who seal the covenant with Nehemiah, committing the restored people to obey the Law of Moses. In Nehemiah 12:14, he is cited again as the head of a priestly house, successor to the lineage of Malchijah, showing his role in the organization of worship and the religious community of rebuilt Jerusalem.
H7645I.origine: The name Schebania means "increased by Jehovah" or "Jehovah has increased." It is composed of the divine element "Yah" (God) and a root evoking increase or growth. This type of name, common in Israel, expresses trust in divine blessing and gratitude towards God. The name reflects the faith of the people in the protection and prosperity granted by the Lord.
H7645I.emploi: Schebania appears twice in the records of Nehemiah related to the period of the return from exile (around the 5th century B.C.). The first mention, in Nehemiah 10:4, shows him among the signatories of the covenant document that formalizes the people's commitment to God and the Law. The second, in Nehemiah 12:14, identifies him as a representative of a priestly family, illustrating the importance of religious structures in the restored community. These two occurrences highlight his role as a spiritual and civil leader in post-exilic Jerusalem.
H7645I.portee: Schebania embodies the faithfulness of religious leaders to the restoration of the community of Israel after the exile. His commitment to seal the covenant and his priestly service remind us that returning to God involves leaders who commit themselves and lead the people. His story shows how God uses ordinary men to rebuild His people and worship, inviting the reader to recognize the place of faithful leaders in the building of the faith community.

sens: Levite who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H7645J.detail: 1. Schébania is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile and the restoration of worship in Jerusalem. His name appears in the list of chief Levites who affixed their seal to the covenant document that the people made with Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:12), thus solemnly committing to observe the Law of Moses.
H7645J.origine: The name Schébania literally means "increased by the Lord" (from the Hebrew *shba* = to increase or add, and *Yah* = God). It is a typical theophoric name from the time of the return from exile, expressing gratitude to God for the restoration and protection of the people after the destruction of Jerusalem.
H7645J.emploi: Schébania appears only once in the preserved biblical texts: in Nehemiah 10:12, among the signatories of the covenant. He is listed among the Levites who participated in the communal religious life after the return from Babylon. His presence in this list shows his role as a religious leader and his authority within the restored community.

sens: To be filled with food, to have eaten to satisfaction
To be fulfilled, satisfied with a desire or want
To fully enjoy something, to have it in abundance
To be overwhelmed, to have too much of something
To enrich, to generously provide
H7646.detail:
1. To be filled with food, to have eaten to satisfaction: the primary meaning is that of a satisfied belly after a meal. Exodus 16:8 speaks of the bread given "to satisfaction," meaning in sufficient quantity for everyone to be fully filled.

2. To be fulfilled, satisfied with a desire or want: the word extends to any desire or need of the heart. Ecclesiastes 6:3 asks if a man's soul can be satisfied with happiness — in other words, is there enough earthly goods to fill the heart?

3. To fully enjoy something, to have it in abundance: this means to receive as much as one desires. Psalms 91:16 promises to satisfy someone with long days, meaning to grant him a full measure.

4. To be overwhelmed, to have too much of something: when satisfaction becomes excessive or disgusting. Job 9:18 describes one who is filled with bitterness, meaning he has had it to the point of nausea.

5. To enrich, to generously provide: to make someone enjoy abundance, especially of material goods. Proverbs 12:14 states that one is satisfied with goods by the fruit of his mouth, in other words enriched by his words.
H7646.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of fullness and saturation. It is linked to the concrete image of a belly filled after a meal. The word belongs to a rich family: the noun "satisfaction" (the condition of being filled) is found in several passages. The root expresses both physical satisfaction and, by natural extension, moral or spiritual satisfaction.
H7646.emploi: This verb appears 93 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (more than twenty occurrences), Proverbs, and historical books. In the Psalms, it constantly recurs: God satisfies the righteous with His goods, joy, and long years (Psalms 17:15, 91:16, 103:5). In Proverbs, it speaks of what fills us: the fruit of our actions, our words, our endeavors (Proverbs 12:14, 14:14). Sometimes the meaning becomes critical: one can be filled with bitterness (Job 9:18), with ungodliness (Jeremiah 5:7), which shows that one absorbs without limit what corrupts the soul. Ecclesiastes raises an existential question: can one really be filled with happiness or earthly possessions? (Ecclesiastes 1:8, 6:3). The verb is also used in the active sense (God satisfies someone): it then emphasizes divine generosity.
H7646.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is the source of abundance and true satisfaction. It invites reflection on what truly fills us: physical food is not enough (Ecclesiastes 6:3), but justice, wisdom, and communion with God fulfill the soul. It also warns: one can be filled with evil as easily as with good. It is a word of mercy and also of warning: seek satisfaction in God first.

sens: Profusion, excessive quantity of food or goods
State of satiation, fullness after being filled
Prosperity and material wealth
H7647.detail:
1. Abundance, first of all, is concrete profusion: much harvest, much grain, much of what fills the granaries. In Pharaoh's dream, the seven years of great abundance produce so much wheat that the land overflows (Genesis 41:29). It is a visible wealth, which accumulates and can be counted.
2. It is also the state of one who has eaten to satisfaction and desires no more: the fulfillment, the fullness of a filled belly. When one has abundance, one is no longer hungry, one has no more need.
3. In a broader sense, it is the prosperity and wealth of a land or a household: when the granaries overflow and everything is going well, it is abundance (Proverbs 3:10). This word paints a life where lacking nothing has become normal.
H7647.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the satisfaction of a filled belly. In Hebrew, this same family is used to express the idea of being filled, full, contented. The basic image is physical: it is the body that has had enough, that is almost overflowing. The word then extends to everything that produces this satisfaction: abundant food, riches, fertile land.
H7647.emploi: The word appears eight times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis 41, at the heart of the story of Pharaoh's dream about the seven fat cows and the seven lean cows. Joseph interprets this dream: seven years of abundance will come, followed by seven years of famine (Genesis 41:29-34). Here, abundance specifically refers to the extraordinary harvest of prosperous years, so rich that it is believed to be inexhaustible until famine arrives. The word reappears in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes to evoke material wealth and fullness.
H7647.portee: This word reminds us that earthly abundance is a gift, but also that it can blind us. The story of Pharaoh teaches that even the greatest prosperity can disappear; it invites us not to build our security on visible riches alone, but to prepare the soul for difficult times that may arise. It is an invitation to wisdom: enjoy the present without believing it will last forever.

sens: State of one who has eaten well, who is no longer hungry
Quantity of food sufficient to satisfy
Abundance, fullness of goods or joys
H7648.detail:
1. Satiety is primarily a full belly, the state of one who has eaten enough to no longer be hungry. The Israelites in the desert regretted having "eaten bread to satiety" in Egypt (Exodus 16:3), meaning they had access to food in sufficient quantity.
2. The word also designates the provision itself, that which satisfies: when one can "eat to satiety" of bread or fruits, it means there is abundance (Leviticus 25:19 and 26:5). Ruth takes "the leftovers of her meal" to her mother-in-law (Ruth 2:18), showing that she had enough to eat her share.
3. Figuratively, the word opens up to all forms of abundance and fullness: God offers "abundant joys" in His presence (Psalms 16:11), a wealth of blessings beyond mere physical well-being.
H7648.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be filled, to be satisfied." It evokes the idea of saturation, of completeness: when one has drunk to satiety, when one has eaten to satiety, nothing is lacking. It is a concrete word that primarily speaks to the body and its basic needs, before extending to spiritual well-being and the lasting joys that God offers.
H7648.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Law and wisdom texts. It is closely related to the Covenant and the promises: to the blessings that God grants to His people when they obey Him (Leviticus 25:19, 26:5 speaks of satiety as the fruit of faithfulness and security). The context of the desert (Exodus 16:3) also shows how the absence of satiety becomes a temptation, a reason for revolt. Finally, the poetry of the Psalms transposes the word to the realm of spiritual joys (Psalms 16:11), showing that satiety can also be that of the soul before God.
H7648.portee: Satiety reminds us of a deep human need: not only to be free from hunger, but to enjoy abundance and security. It is also a divine promise: those who trust in God are not left in want. Finally, it invites us to go beyond the physical: true lasting joys come from the presence of God, not from reserves of grain or bread.

sens: Filled, satisfied, to satiety
Abundantly provided, filled with blessings
Satisfied with days: who has lived long and fully
Excess, overload (pejorative sense)
H7649.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who has eaten to satiety, who is full: "Those who were full praise for bread" (1 Samuel 2:5) means that those who had an abundance of food must now beg to eat.
2. It extends to everything that fills and satisfies: to be satisfied with favors, with blessings, is to be abundantly provided (Deuteronomy 33:23).
3. The expression "satisfied with days" is a biblical way of saying that a person has lived a long and fulfilling life: "Abraham breathed his last and died, after a good old age, old and satisfied with days" (Genesis 25:8) means he had a full and satisfying life.
4. The word can also express an unpleasant overload or excess: Job says, "Satiated with shame and absorbed in my misery" (Job 10:15), expressing that he is overwhelmed by shame and suffering, like someone who can bear no more.
H7649.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to fill" or "to gorge." It evokes the image of someone whose belly, soul, or heart is filled to the brim. The same root gives words from the family of satisfaction and fullness. This Hebrew word corresponds in Greek to the term "plērēs" (filled) or "kekoros" (satisfied).
H7649.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in death narratives (Genesis 25:8; 35:29; 1 Chronicles 29:28) to express a well-lived and happy life. It also appears in poetic passages: the Psalms and Proverbs use it to speak of the satisfaction that the Lord provides (Deuteronomy 33:23; Proverbs 19:23). In the book of Job, it takes on a darker shade, designating an excess of suffering or shame (Job 10:15). The use of "satisfied with days" has become almost a biblical cliché to describe a happy death after a long life, like that of Abraham or David.
H7649.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that true satisfaction comes not from food or possessions, but from communion with God and His blessings. The expression "satisfied with days" invites us to desire a full life in the presence of God, rather than a mere existence. It teaches that true rest and fullness are a gift from God for those who fear Him.

sens: Make a solemn commitment invoking God as a witness
Promise something under oath, commit by word
Take an oath of obedience or loyalty to someone
Affirm the truth of something by swearing
Curse oneself if one does not keep one's word
H7650.detail:
1. To swear is to make a solemn promise invoking God as a witness. Abraham said to Abimelech: "I will swear it" (Genesis 21:24), meaning he swears to uphold an agreement. It is the most serious gesture to engage one's honor and conscience.
2. Often, the one who swears promises something specific: an act, an obedience, the possession of land. God Himself "swears" in the sense that He makes a solemn commitment to give His servants the land He has promised: "I had sworn to our fathers, this land flowing with milk and honey" (Deuteronomy 26:15).
3. One can also swear loyalty to a person or accept their authority. Jehoiada "made the military leaders swear" in the temple, meaning he compelled them to commit by oath to support the king (2 Kings 11:4).
4. To swear can mean to solemnly affirm that something is true: one who "swears" falsely commits a grave sin (Leviticus 19:12).
5. Implicitly, to swear is to curse oneself if one does not keep one's word: one calls upon God's punishment in case of perjury.
H7650.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁבַע (shava') likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of "seven" (שׁבע, sheva), as the ancient formula of oath involved seven gestures or seven words. To swear is thus to perform a sevenfold act, highly formal and irrevocable. The noun "oath" (שְׁבוּעָה, shebuah) comes from the same root.
H7650.emploi: This verb appears 175 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. It primarily describes oaths between men: Abraham swears with Abimelech (Genesis 21), Jacob and Laban swear loyalty to each other (Genesis 31:53). But the richest usage is that of the divine oath: God swears to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give them the promised land — this oath recurs dozens of times in Deuteronomy and Joshua, founding the entire history of the Hebrew people. Swearing is also a human duty: one must swear by the name of the Lord (Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:20), that is, invoke His authority as a guarantee. Finally, swearing falsely is a grave crime that pollutes the temple and the community.
H7650.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God is not only powerful but faithful: His oath stands forever. It is a source of assurance for those who have faith in His promises. In return, swearing oneself before God is a daunting responsibility: one should only swear to speak the truth, and one must never fail to keep one's word given before God. It is a call to sincerity and honesty of heart.

sens: The number 7, cardinal number
Used as an ordinal number: the seventh
Used in composition to form other numbers: 17, 70, 700, etc.
H7651.detail:
1. The number 7 is the most common in the Bible to express a quantity: the seven years of abundance and the seven years of famine from Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41), the seven days of Passover (Exodus 12:19), or simply enumerations like the seven daughters of the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16). It is a number that biblical authors use without particular symbolism, as one would today.
2. The number 7 also functions as an ordinal, to designate the seventh rank or the seventh occurrence: the seventh day of creation, or the order of succession in an enumeration.
3. In compound numbers, 7 adds to other digits to form larger ones: seventy-seven times (Genesis 4:24) or seven hundred (Nehemiah 7:29). The word fits into these combinations without losing its base value.
H7651.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁבַע comes from an ancient root denoting the number 7, common to Semitic languages. In biblical Aramaic, we find שִׁבְעָה (shiv'ah) with the same meaning. The number 7 holds particular importance in the Bible and in ancient Near Eastern culture, often associated with the idea of completeness or totality, but the word itself is primarily a simple cardinal number.
H7651.emploi: The word שֶׁבַע appears more than 346 times in the Hebrew Bible, making it one of the most frequent numbers. It appears in almost all historical, legal, and poetic books. In Genesis 41, it describes the cows and ears of grain in Pharaoh's dream. In Exodus 12, it measures the duration of Passover. In Leviticus, it delineates the periods of purification or confinement (Leviticus 13:4-5). The word is also used for the ages of the patriarchs (Genesis 5:25 for Methuselah) or the periods of service (Genesis 29:27 for Jacob and Laban). Its usage is strictly numerical: the text never invests it with hidden or symbolic meaning at the word level.
H7651.portee: Knowing this number and its uses helps the reader grasp biblical structures: the cycles of seven days, the seven-year sabbatical years, or the cultic measures that recur constantly. It also connects them to the concrete reality of the text, far from easy allegorizing. For the believer, recognizing these numerical repetitions in the text invites them to see how God orders time and durations according to a design, while remaining faithful to the letter of the narrative.

sens: Benjamite who led a revolt against King David
Gadite mentioned in genealogical lists
H7652A.detail: 1. Sheba is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bichri, who rose against King David during the period of the united monarchy. After Absalom's revolt, he took advantage of the discontent of the northern Israelites to call for secession: "We have no share in David, nor do we have an inheritance in the son of Jesse!" (2 Samuel 20:1). He is portrayed as a rebel who caused serious troubles, to the point that David compared him to an enemy more dangerous than Absalom himself (2 Samuel 20:6). 2. A second Sheba is mentioned as a Gadite, brother of Michael, Meshullam, and others, appearing in the genealogical lists of the Gadites.
H7652A.origine: The name Sheba means "seven" in Hebrew. It is a patronymic name that appears in the Hebrew text as שֶׁ֫בַע. In the Bible, numerical names can have symbolic significance or simply identify an individual. The name is borne by several different people, which was common in ancient Israel.
H7652A.emploi: Sheba the Benjamite appears 6 times in 2 Samuel 20, a chapter entirely devoted to his revolt. Shortly after the suppression of Absalom's revolt, this Benjamite leader sounded the trumpet to mobilize the men of Israel against David, seeking to separate from the kingdom. The northern tribes followed him, while Judah remained loyal to the king (2 Samuel 20:2). David sent his generals, Joab and Abishai, to pursue him (2 Samuel 20:7 and 20:10), and he was ultimately killed at Abel-Bet-Maacah, where the city's inhabitants delivered his head to Joab (2 Samuel 20:21-22). Sheba the Gadite appears only once, in a genealogical list of the families of Gad, without particular narrative context.
H7652A.portee: The revolt of Sheba illustrates the fragility of Israelite unity under David and shows how tensions between the northern and southern tribes could escalate into secession. His story reminds us that obedience to the king established by God is more important than personal ambition or tribal divisions. For the Christian, this passage teaches the dangers of division and the necessity of the unity of God's people.

sens: City of the tribe of Simeon, in Canaan
H7652B.detail: Sheba is a city that was allotted to the tribe of Simeon during the division of the promised land. Its name means "seven" in Hebrew, and it is another name for Beersheba, the famous city in the South. The Bible mentions it in the enumeration of the cities of Simeon (Joshua 19:2), where it appears among the localities that this tribe received as an inheritance.
H7652B.origine: The name Sheba literally means "seven" in Hebrew. It is another designation for Beersheba ("well of the oath"), an ancient and important city in the Negev. The name may evoke either the seven wells of the region or an event related to the number seven, according to local traditions.
H7652B.emploi: Sheba appears only once in the Segond, in Joshua 19:2, where it is listed among the cities that the tribe of Simeon inherited during the division of Canaan. This mention is part of the administrative list of territorial possessions of each tribe, which occupies an important place in the book of Joshua.

sens: A man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy of Israel
H7652G.detail: Sheba is a man of the tribe of Gad, whose name literally means "seven." He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, where he is listed among the sons of Abihail with his brothers Michael, Meshullam, Jorai, Jaecan, Zia, and Eber. Living during the time of the divided monarchy (after the separation of the kingdom of Israel into two kingdoms) places this man in a pivotal period of Israel's history. He represents one of the notable families of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel established east of the Jordan.
H7652G.origine: The name Sheba means "seven" in Hebrew, which recalls the importance of the number seven in biblical culture — a number of completion, perfection, or totality. This name was borne by at least two biblical figures: this Sheba of Gad and a city of the same name in the territory of Simeon. The choice of the number seven for a name often reveals a religious significance or a blessing in the ancient Hebrew mindset.
H7652G.emploi: Sheba appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Gad. This mention is part of a register intended to preserve the memory of families and their lineages, as was common at the time of the return from Babylonian exile. The genealogical context shows that Sheba was a man of responsibility and status in his tribe, as he is named alongside his brothers in this official compilation.

sens: State of one who has eaten or drunk to their fill
Abundance or profusion of material goods
Complete and total satisfaction of desires
H7653.detail:
1. Satiation is primarily the physical state of one who has eaten or drunk enough and is no longer hungry or thirsty. It is to have one's fill, to be satisfied. In Ezekiel 16:49, Jerusalem is accused of pride precisely because it lives in abundance: it has everything in excess, lacking nothing.
2. The word also refers to the material abundance itself, the provisions and riches that fulfill needs. When one is satiated, it means they possess in sufficient, even overflowing, quantity.
3. Finally, it can evoke complete satisfaction, the moment when the heart is at peace because nothing is lacking. But the Bible shows that this material satiation often hides a spiritual emptiness: having everything does not mean being fulfilled in a deeper sense.
H7653.origine: The Hebrew word siv'ah comes from a root that means "to be satisfied" or "to be filled." It belongs to the same family as the verb that describes the action of eating to satisfaction. Its primary image is that of a filled stomach, a satisfied belly, before it more broadly designates any state of abundance and fullness.
H7653.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 16:49. It is part of the long condemnation that the prophet pronounces against Jerusalem: the city has known prosperity, peace, abundance, and it is precisely in this state of material satiation that it has become proud and forgotten the poor. The context shows that satiation is not in itself evil, but it becomes dangerous when it hardens the heart and turns one away from God.
H7653.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on their relationship with wealth and goods. Material satiation is a spiritual danger: it can make us forget our dependence on God and render us indifferent to those who suffer. It is a call to remain vigilant when life is going well, not to let abundance extinguish our sensitivity to justice and mercy.

sens: state of one who has eaten to their fill, who no longer desires food
state of one who is satisfied, fulfilled in a desire
H7654.detail:
1. Satiation is the physical state of one who has eaten until they are no longer hungry. It is that feeling of fullness and satisfaction when one has had enough food. In Ezekiel 39:19, the people will eat "fat until you are satisfied," an image of abundance where everyone can eat to their fill.
2. Figuratively, the word denotes the state of one whose desire is fulfilled, complete satisfaction. But the Bible often uses it to highlight dissatisfaction: in Ezekiel 16:28 and Haggai 1:6, the person eats, drinks, strives, but is "not satisfied" — they always desire more, no material abundance truly contenting them.
H7654.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be satisfied, to have enough." It expresses the concrete idea of physical satiation. In Hebrew, there is also the verb from the same family that means "to satisfy" someone. The underlying image is that of filling completely, to satisfaction.
H7654.emploi: This word appears six times in the Old Testament, almost always in the writings of the prophets Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Haggai. It can describe true satiation: abundant food in Isaiah 23:18, the future feast in Ezekiel 39:19. But the Bible mainly uses it to shed light on the absence of satiation: Isaiah 55:2 invites not to seek satisfaction in what does not "satisfy," and Haggai 1:6 shows a people who eat without being "satisfied," who work without profit — an image of a spiritually empty life, without blessing.
H7654.portee: This word reminds us that only God can truly satisfy us. Wealth, worldly pleasures, idolatry — none of these fill the human heart. It is a warning against the perpetual pursuit of material goods: a man can possess much and remain "insatiable." Conversely, one who turns to the Lord finds in Him the true satisfaction that nothing can take away.
