sens: The number 7, expressing a precise quantity of objects or people
A duration or interval of time repeated or prolonged
A number symbolizing divine order or fullness in God's purpose
H7655.detail:
1. Seven is primarily the whole number that follows six. In Ezra 7:14, the king sends seven counselors to inspect Judah: it is a concrete quantity of people. It is also the number of times the furnace must be heated (Daniel 3:19), a simple counting of repeated actions.
2. Seven can designate a period of time: seven times or seven years. In Daniel 4, God announces that Nebuchadnezzar will live seven times like a beast (4:16 and 4:32), an image of prolonged and divine humiliation. The number here is not just a statistic, but measures the duration of punishment.
3. The number 7 carries a deep meaning in the Bible: it often expresses the fulfillment of God's will. The repetition of the number "seven times" in the account of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:16, 4:23, 4:25, 4:32) emphasizes that this trial is not random, but order and purpose of the Most High.
H7655.origine: This Aramaic word שִׁבְעָה (shiv'ah) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word שֶׁבַע (sheva, seven) from number H7651. In Aramaic, as in Hebrew, seven was fundamental: it structured sacred cycles (weeks, sabbatical years, jubilees). The number 7 appears from Creation (Genesis 2:3, the seventh day) and traverses the Old Testament as a number of order, completeness, and divine blessing.
H7655.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only 6 times, all in the Aramaic portions of Daniel (3:19) and Ezra (7:14 and Daniel 4). In Daniel 4, it appears four times to describe the "seven times" during which Nebuchadnezzar will be humiliated and live like a beast of the field — a punishment whose duration and fulfillment God measures. The context always shows that the number 7 is not accidental: it is God who sets it to accomplish His purposes. In Ezra 7:14, the number 7 simply marks the official composition of a royal delegation.
H7655.portee: The number seven reminds the reader that God controls time and history, even when He punishes. The "seven times" of Nebuchadnezzar are not a blind curse, but a measured and just judgment of the Most High. For the Christian, this number symbolizes that nothing escapes God's control: His purposes are realized precisely, and His judgments are just and limited in time.

sens: Well named by Isaac near Beersheba
H7656.detail: Schiba is the name of a well dug by Isaac and his servants. The name means "oath" in Hebrew, as Isaac named it in remembrance of the peace treaty made with Abimelech, king of the Philistines. This well was located in the region of Beersheba, in the Negev (Genesis 26:33).
H7656.origine: The Hebrew name Schiba comes from the root שָׁבַע (shaba), which means "to swear" or "to make an oath." This same root also produced the word שֶׁבַע (sheba), which designates the number seven. In ancient Hebrew, to make an oath was literally said as "to make seven" or "to commit by seven," hence the link between the oath and the number seven. The well of Schiba received its name due to the covenant oath that the men had just made.
H7656.emploi: Schiba appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:33. Isaac had dug a well and made a peace treaty with Abimelech. To immortalize this oath, he named the well "Schiba" (the Oath). This well was located very near Beersheba (literally "the Well of the Oath"), which explains why the two names are associated. The origin of the name Beersheba is thus linked to this significant event in patriarchal history.

sens: The number 70, composed of seven times ten
A number symbolizing totality, fulfillment, or completeness
A number expressing a large quantity, a multitude
A number marking a period or duration in life
H7657.detail:
1. Seventy is primarily a simple cardinal number: 7 × 10. It appears in concrete counts of people or goods — for instance, Solomon counted seventy thousand men to bear burdens (2 Chronicles 2:2), or the descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt were seventy souls (Genesis 46:27).
2. The number 70 carries symbolic significance: it represents the fulfillment or totality of a work. When God tells Moses to choose seventy elders to share the burden of governance (Numbers 11:16-25), this number is not arbitrary — it marks a complete and divine structure of the people. Similarly, Cain's curse, which will be avenged "seventy-seven times" (Genesis 4:24), expresses an unlimited and thus definitive vengeance.
3. Seventy also serves to designate a large crowd: the seventy sons of Jerubbaal (Judges 9:2-5) embody a massive family power. It is a number that stands out due to its magnitude in the context of the ancient world.
4. In terms of ages or durations, seventy years marks the limit of a human life: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten" (Psalms 90:10). Tyre must also remain forgotten for seventy years (Isaiah 23:15), marking a complete cycle of punishment and restoration.
H7657.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁבְעִים (shiv'im) derives from the root שׁ-ב-ע which means "seven." Seventy is therefore literally "ten times seven." This numerical construction follows the Hebrew system: like the Greek ἑβδομήκοντα, it combines the unit seven (שׁבע) and the base ten. The number 7 carries a strong symbolic weight in Israel — perfection, totality, holiness — and the multiple 70 naturally amplifies its spiritual resonance.
H7657.emploi: Seventy appears about 90 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in historical books and census accounts. In the Pentateuch, it arises during military counts (Numbers 1:27: seventy-four thousand men of Judah) or population counts (Genesis 46:27: the families of Jacob). In Judges, the number carries dramatic weight: the seventy sons of Jerubbaal embody dynastic power, and their massacre (Judges 9) becomes a breaking point in the narrative. The number also appears in counts of royal workers under David and Solomon, marking the extent of their administrative power. Finally, seventy years mark entire periods of exile or restoration (2 Chronicles 36:21), reinforcing the idea that this number closes a divine cycle.
H7657.portee: The number seventy reveals to the reader that God orders and counts His people with precision: every soul matters to Him, and the organization of Israel responds to a numerical and theological design, not to chance. Seeing seventy elders or seventy representatives is never neutral — it is participating in the fulfillment of a structure intended by God. By mentioning seventy years as the limit of life (Psalms 90), the text teaches humility in the face of human finitude and the eternity of God.

sens: The whole number that comes after six and before eight
H7658.detail: 1. The number seven, in its purely numerical sense: it is the digit that designates a precise quantity of objects or people. In the text of Job, this number qualifies the sons that Job had after his trial: "He had seven sons and three daughters" (Job 42:13). Here it is merely a simple count.
H7658.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁבְעָ֫נָה (shivah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of completeness and fullness. In Hebrew, the number seven carries particular spiritual significance, often linked to divine fulfillment and perfection: one thinks of creation in seven days, the seven years of plenty and famine, or forgiving seven times. The word is from the family of the verb שׁבע which means "to swear," as swearing is to commit completely, totally.
H7658.emploi: The word appears once in the provided usages, in Job 42:13, where it simply denotes the number of Job's sons. This figure, in the context of Job, carries a deeper meaning: it symbolizes Job's complete and abundant restoration after his sufferings. The number seven in the Bible often bears a significance beyond mere arithmetic calculation.
H7658.portee: The number seven in Job's life represents full and complete divine restoration. It reminds readers that God does not restore halfway: He multiplies and fills beyond measure. Seeing the number seven in Job's story invites reflection on divine generosity and how God restores what has been lost.

sens: The number seven repeated or multiplied by itself
A quantity or intensity increased radically
A vengeance, a punishment, or a reparation multiplied
A purity or perfection brought to its peak
H7659.detail:
1. The word first designates the number seven taken as a multiplier: seven times more of something, or seven times as much. In Genesis 4:15, God decrees that Cain will be avenged "sevenfold" — not that he will be killed once, but that anyone who kills him will be punished infinitely more severely.
2. This multiplication expresses a radical, almost superhuman intensification. In Isaiah 30:26, the light of the sun becomes "seven times brighter," which depicts the wonderful brightness of the day of healing: it means it will be extraordinarily radiant, far beyond a normal day.
3. In contexts of justice and vengeance, the term signifies a multiplied retribution. In Psalms 79:12, one asks God to repay "sevenfold" to the enemies the outrages they have committed — a vigorous way of asking for punishment commensurate with the crime.
4. Applied to purity, "seven times refined" (Psalms 12:7) expresses the absolute excellence of God's words: tested, proven, refined to the ultimate perfection, like silver in the crucible.
H7659.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שָׁבַע (shava), which means "seven." It is formed in the dual or plural to express the repetition or multiplication of the sacred number. The number seven carries a strong symbolic weight in biblical Hebrew: it evokes perfection, fulfillment, divine completeness. Multiplying by seven thus means "well beyond ordinary measure, according to a divine order."
H7659.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in poetic books and ancient narratives. In Genesis 4:15-24, it is used in the context of Cain's curse and Lamech's vendetta, expressing an excessive vengeance. In the Psalms (12:7 and 79:12), it qualifies either the purified purity of divine words or the expected retribution of enemies. In Proverbs 6:31 and Isaiah 30:26, it indicates a sevenfold restitution or an incomparable light. In each case, the meaning oscillates between perfection, extreme intensity, and disproportionate vengeance.
H7659.portee: This word reminds the reader that God acts according to a logic that surpasses simple equivalence or human fairness. When He promises vengeance "sevenfold," He asserts that His judgment infinitely surpasses the offense — a comfort for the persecuted believer. But also a warning: to engage in conflict against God or His people carries amplified consequences. Elsewhere, the expression exalts divine perfection: His words are never tainted, His light will one day transform the universe beyond all we can imagine.

sens: to fix a precious stone in a setting
to insert or weave elements into a structure
to assemble pieces tightly and orderly
H7660.detail:
1. The primary meaning describes the action of securely fixing a precious stone in a metal setting: one sets the stone so that it is well held and shines in its place. In Exodus 28:20, the stones of the high priest's breastplate are "set in their gold settings" — each has its assigned place in the gold structure that holds them.
2. The word also evokes weaving or insertion: fine threads or elements are interwoven or "woven" to form a structured whole. In Exodus 28:39, the verb applies to the making of priestly garments, where colored and gold threads are incorporated into the linen tunic according to a specific pattern — it is a work of insertion and assembly, like stones in a setting.
3. The overall image is one of organized and lasting insertion: the elements are not placed vaguely, but attached, incorporated, "set" into a coherent and orderly whole.
H7660.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁבץ (sha­vats) initially denotes the action of weaving or interlacing in regular patterns. Its biblical context associates it with fine works: the weaving of brocade, the incorporation of stones into priestly ornaments, the insertion of gold and colored threads into worship garments. The root evokes the idea of placing something within a complex and orderly structure. The verb primarily appears in the context of the high priest's ornaments — a domain requiring precision and beauty.
H7660.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible (Exodus 28:20 and 28:39). Both occurrences concern the high priest's equipment: first, the precious stones of the breastplate, then the priestly garments (tunic, tiara, belt). In the first case, it refers to the setting in gold; in the second, to the making of the garments with their woven and adorned elements. The word is thus limited to the priestly domain and fine craftsmanship — it is a term of trade, rare and highly specialized.
H7660.portee: This word reminds us that the worship offered to God requires precision, care, and order. Each stone has its place, each gold thread its pattern: holiness is also expressed through the excellence of work and organized beauty. For the Christian, this invites us to consider that what we offer to God — our time, our heart, our actions — deserves to be shaped with intention and attention, not done lightly.

sens: A sensation of spinning, dizziness that seizes the body
A state of intense physical anxiety or discomfort
Mental confusion caused by suffering or distress
H7661.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a physical sensation of spinning or dizziness — the type of malaise that causes loss of balance and disturbs vision. It is a concrete symptom of the body.
2. It can also describe deep anxiety, an existential discomfort: it is the sensation that everything is spinning around oneself, that the ground is giving way. In the key text (2 Samuel 1:9), the wounded warrior says he is "seized by dizziness" while he is still alive — he speaks of the state of confusion and distress that overwhelms him in the face of his imminent death.
3. The word finally encompasses the idea of a mental disturbance caused by suffering, an emotional disruption that disorients.
H7661.origine: The exact etymology of this Hebrew word remains uncertain. It belongs to a small group of biblical terms describing states of physical and mental discomfort. The biblical context suggests a connection with the idea of something that spins or troubles, but the precise link with other words in the same family is not firmly established.
H7661.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 1:9. It is Agag, the king of the Amalekites, who utters it: mortally wounded in battle, he asks the one who has defeated him to end his agony. He literally says he is "seized by dizziness" while he is still alive. This unique occurrence reveals how the Hebrews spoke of the deep malaise that accompanies imminent death — a disturbance that is both physical and emotional, a state where the body and mind lose their bearings.
H7661.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks of human agony without reservation. It acknowledges the reality of dizziness, confusion, and loss of balance in the face of death. This invites us to meditate on the vulnerability of the body and to seek in God a stability that the world cannot provide.

sens: To allow someone or something to continue, to exist without intervening
To abandon, to cease holding or maintaining
To let remain, to leave intact
H7662.detail:
1. To allow someone or something to continue, to exist without intervening — it is not to prevent an action or situation. In Ezra 6:7, the king orders to "leave" the temple work to continue: it is about not stopping them, allowing them to proceed. In Daniel 2:44, the kingdom of God "will not pass" under the dominion of another people — it will never be handed over to someone else, never delivered to an enemy.
2. To abandon, to cease holding or maintaining — it is to release the grip, to let go of what one was holding. When one "binds" the trunk of the tree with chains (Daniel 4:15, 4:23), this binding holds it; to "leave" would mean to free it from this constraint. It is an image of detention and liberation.
3. To let remain, to leave intact — it is to decide not to destroy or annihilate. In Daniel's vision, it is ordered to cut down the tree but to "leave" the trunk with its roots in the ground (Daniel 4:23, 4:26): a part is preserved while the rest is destroyed. This nuance expresses a partial intervention: some things disappear, others remain.
H7662.origine: This Aramaic verb belongs to the family of words that express the idea of releasing or letting go. The root expresses a certain passivity or absence of action — to let something follow its course or remain as it is. The verb conjugates in two main forms: the simple form (P'al) marks the action of the subject who "leaves," and the passive form (Ithpael) describes the state of the one or that which "is left." This structure reflects a conception where "to leave" is both an action (negative intervention) and a condition (the state of that which remains).
H7662.emploi: This verb appears five times in biblical Aramaic, concentrated in the books of Ezra and Daniel, two historical and prophetic texts of the return from exile. In Ezra 6:7, it expresses the king's order to allow the reconstruction of the temple. In Daniel 2:44, it refers to the eternal kingdom of God that will never be ceded to an earthly power. In Daniel 4:15, 4:23, and 4:26, the word appears in the vision of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the trunk must be "left" in the ground, which means that despite the cutting down of the tree, a root remains — an image of the royalty that will persist after the king's humiliation. The usages highlight a tension between destruction and preservation, authorization and refusal.
H7662.portee: This word reminds the reader that God intervenes in history: He "leaves" kingdoms to rise and fall, He "leaves" alive what will remain according to His plan. It is a word that liberates — God allows His people to rebuild their temple — and reassures — even in judgment, God preserves a root. For the Christian, "to leave" also evokes the freedom that God grants us to choose, while remaining under His sovereignty.

sens: Examine carefully, look closely
Inspect the details of something to judge its condition
Reflect on what one observes
H7663A.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to look at something attentively, paying attention to details. It is the act of one who wants to truly see and understand what they observe. In Nehemiah 2:13, Nehemiah goes out at night to "consider" the ruined walls of Jerusalem: he looks closely at the state of the walls to assess the extent of the damage.

2. It then denotes the inspection of something in detail, to judge its state or condition. It is a methodical examination, not just a cursory glance. Nehemiah "considers" the wall while going up at night by the brook (Nehemiah 2:15), seeking to see for himself what reconstruction work is necessary.

3. The word can also evoke the reflection that accompanies this observation: while looking at the ruined walls, Nehemiah reflects on what he sees and begins to conceive his restoration project. It is the examination that leads to understanding and decision-making.
H7663A.origine: The root שׂבר evokes the idea of looking, observing carefully. It is related to Hebrew words expressing sight and attention. The verb carries the image of a gaze that stops on something to scrutinize it in detail, rather than seeing it in passing. It is a verb of active and thoughtful observation.
H7663A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Nehemiah 2, during the nighttime inspection that the governor conducts around Jerusalem. In this context, Nehemiah "considers" the ruined walls of the holy city to personally ascertain the extent of the destruction and then obtain from the king of Persia the authorization and resources to rebuild them. The usage emphasizes the personal and attentive nature of this inspection: it is a responsible gaze that seeks to understand the situation before acting.
H7663A.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of carefully examining situations before making significant decisions. Like Nehemiah who looks at the ruined walls before getting to work, we are called to observe reality with care and reflection, especially when it comes to serving God or helping others. It is a call to responsibility and clarity in action.

sens: Wait for something with patience
Count on someone or something for the future
Turn one's gaze or desire towards someone or something
H7663B.detail:
1. To wait for something with patience: the word evokes the idea of remaining in expectation, in suspense, waiting for a future event. Naomi asks her daughters-in-law: "Would you wait for them to grow up?" (Ruth 1:13), meaning: would you stay here hoping that my sons grow up? It is an active waiting, tinged with doubt or fear.
2. To count on someone or something for the future: to hope is to place one's trust in someone or something that can meet a need or fulfill a desire. The animals "hope in you, to give them their food" (Psalms 104:27): they turn their expectation towards God, certain that He will provide. The psalmist "hopes in your salvation" (Psalms 119:166), firmly counting on the help of the Lord.
3. To turn one's gaze or desire towards someone or something: hoping includes the image of a visible expectation, an anticipation that can be read on the face. "The eyes of all hope in you" (Psalms 145:15) gives a concrete image: all lift their eyes towards God in expectation. To the enemies of the Jews who "had hoped to dominate" (Esther 9:1), the deliverance of the Lord disappointed this malicious hope.
H7663B.origine: The root שׁ-ב-ר (s-b-r) fundamentally expresses the idea of "looking towards" or "waiting with intensity." It appears mainly in biblical Hebrew in the Piel form (intensive form of the verb), reinforcing the sense of an ardent expectation, a trust that relies heavily on someone. The related Aramaic סְבַר (sevar) means "to intend" or "to have the intention," showing that the root carries the idea of directing one's mind towards something. In the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word often conveys the idea of waiting and hoping in God.
H7663B.emploi: The verb שׁ-ב-ר appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly used in the Psalms and historical narratives. It always denotes an expectation or trust directed towards someone or something. In the Psalms, it is the confident expectation directed towards God: the believer "hopes in your salvation" (119:166), the creatures "hope in you" (104:27; 145:15). In Isaiah 38:18, the context is reversed: the dead "no longer hope in your faithfulness," for death cuts them off from any communion with the living God. In the historical narratives, Ruth 1:13 and Esther 9:1, the word describes an earthly expectation, whether disillusioned or malicious. The word is only found in the conjugated verb form, never as an abstract noun.
H7663B.portee: This word invites the believer to turn their gaze towards God, not to settle for a vague expectation but to place their active trust in Him. Biblical hope is not a passive wish, but an expectation grounded in the known faithfulness of God. To know how to hope in God is to recognize that He provides, that He keeps His promises, and to live this certainty even in trials: the psalmist hopes in God not because everything is going well, but because God is trustworthy.

sens: Confident expectation in a promise from God
Inner certainty that God will act according to His word
Foundation of the believer's life
H7664.detail:
1. Hope is the living and confident expectation of what God has promised. It is not a vague thought or an uncertain wish, but a certainty anchored in God Himself. The psalmist says: "Uphold me according to your promise, that I may live, and do not let me be put to shame in my hope" (Psalms 119:116) — it is a request to God to support him because his life rests on this trust.
2. Hope is what the believer relies on to live. It gives meaning and courage in the face of trials. One who "puts their hope in the Lord, their God" is declared "blessed" (Psalms 146:5), because this hope connects them to God Himself, the only one who cannot fail.
H7664.origine: The Hebrew word שֵׂ֫בֶר (sèver) comes from a root that evokes the idea of supporting oneself, of attaching to something solid. In biblical Hebrew, hope is never weak or dreamy: it is firm, grounded in the promises and character of God. It is an active trust that stands firm even in adversity.
H7664.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, only in the Book of Psalms. In Psalms 119:116, it denotes the hope of the believer who clings to the word of God to avoid being humiliated. In Psalms 146:5, it describes one who puts their trust in God alone — which makes them "blessed." In both cases, hope is never abstract: it is linked to God's current support and His promise to act. It is the attitude of the psalmist who faces life with assurance because he knows that God keeps His word.
H7664.portee: For the Christian reader, this notion of biblical hope transforms the understanding of faith. It is not human optimism or superstition, but a certainty rooted in God's promises and His unchanging character. Cultivating this hope means accepting to live carried by God's faithfulness rather than by our own strengths or apparent certainties. It is what gives the believer the strength to persevere in trials and to remain "blessed" even when circumstances are difficult.

sens: To break an object into pieces
To shatter, violently destroy
To weaken, nullify someone's strength
To break a bond, a covenant, an obligation
To dominate, conquer (the one who 'breaks' dominates)
H7665.detail:
1. To break an object into pieces: the word describes the action of reducing something to fragments, like a vase that breaks. This is the material and concrete sense: Isaiah compares the destruction of the world to a clay vase that is broken without mercy (Isaiah 30:14).
2. To shatter, violently destroy: this means to break with force and destructive intent, as when people want to break down the door against Lot (Genesis 19:9) or when a lion breaks the bones of its prey.
3. To weaken, nullify someone's strength: the word applies to the body and power: the arms of the wicked "will be broken" (Psalms 37:17), meaning they become powerless; God "breaks the yoke" of Egypt, meaning He destroys its authority (Ezekiel 30:18).
4. To break a bond, a covenant, an obligation: to break also means to annul, to undo. It is to break the chains that bind (Leviticus 26:13) or to destroy idols to break the covenant with false gods (Exodus 23:24).
5. To dominate, conquer: the one who "breaks" exerts overwhelming power over the other. It is the contrast between one who can no longer stand and the one who has brought him down.
H7665.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁבר (sha.var) represents the image of a sharp blow, a crash. It comes from a root that evokes the noise and violent action of separating, dividing by force. In Hebrew, related words revolve around this idea of rupture and destruction. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (used by early Christians), this verb was rendered by the Greek "κλάω" (klao) or "συντρίβω" (syntribō), which have the same range of meanings: to break, to shatter, to crush.
H7665.emploi: The verb "break" appears about 142 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and the Psalms. It first describes very concrete actions: breaking a door (Genesis 19:9), breaking the tablets of the law (Deuteronomy 9:17), breaking idols and altars (Exodus 23:24, 2 Chronicles 34:4). But it quickly extends to the figurative: breaking the power of an enemy, breaking the chains of slavery, breaking a proud heart. God "breaks" the plans of the wicked (Isaiah 8:15) and "breaks" the oppressed to save them (Isaiah 61:1). The Psalms use this verb to cry out to God: "Break the arm of the wicked!" (Psalms 10:15). The word also appears in ceremonial laws: the bone of the Passover lamb must not be broken (Exodus 12:46), an image of wholeness and integrity that the Gospels apply to Christ.
H7665.portee: This word teaches that only God has the power to "break" — either to destroy evil and injustice, or to free captives from their chains. It invites us not to fear those who break the body, but to fear the one who can break pride and the plans of oppressors. For the believer, the word "break" also speaks of the necessity for the flesh to be "broken" (the broken heart, Psalms 51:19) to receive grace and salvation. It is a word of hope: what seems crushed and broken by evil can be restored by divine power.

sens: To acquire grain in exchange for money
To sell grain in exchange for money
To procure food by paying
H7666.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the act of buying wheat or grain: one gives money to receive food. This is what Joseph's brothers do in Egypt: they go down to "buy wheat" in the face of the famine that strikes the land of Canaan (Genesis 42:3).
2. The verb can also mean "to sell grain" — this is the inverse perspective, from the seller's side. Joseph, in Egypt, "sold wheat" to the Egyptians who were suffering from famine (Genesis 41:56). It is the same act viewed from the other side.
3. More broadly, the word denotes the commercial exchange of food for money, whether one is a buyer or a seller. Deuteronomy 2:28 even applies it to water: "You will sell me the food that I will eat for money."
H7666.origine: The Hebrew root שׁבר evokes the idea of breaking or crushing the grain (hence its use for grinding or reducing to crumbs), then by extension the action of procuring grain that is then ground. The word is related to a widely attested Semitic family: the Aramaic زبن (zevan) also means "to buy." The basic image is therefore that of preparing the grain — breaking it, transforming it — before consuming it.
H7666.emploi: This verb appears about 20 times in the Bible, mainly in the account of the famine in Egypt (Genesis 41-44), where Joseph buys and sells wheat. The context is almost always that of subsistence: the buying or selling of food in times of famine or in normal situations. It is also found in the laws of Deuteronomy (buying food and water with payment), in Proverbs 11:26 (he who withholds grain is cursed), and among the prophets (Isaiah 55:1 invites to buy wine and milk without money; Amos 8:5-6 denounces dishonest merchants who buy the poor for wheat). The word applies sometimes to the buyer, sometimes to the seller, depending on the voice of the verb.
H7666.portee: This word reminds us of the vital importance of food and the commerce that arises from it. It also shows how God provides for the needs of His people even in times of crisis: Joseph, an instrument of divine providence, feeds the hungry. For the Christian, the image of purchasable wheat also evokes the invitation of Isaiah 55:1, where the word of God is given freely — it does not need to be "bought." The word invites reflection on subsistence, fair trade, and trust in God.

sens: Fracture or physical injury of the body
Destruction, collapse of a city or building
Disaster, catastrophe, misfortune that strikes
Plague or suffering caused by divine judgment
Interpretation or hidden meaning (of a dream or vision)
H7667.detail:
1. The word first denotes a bone fracture or a serious injury to the body: in Leviticus 21:19, a priest cannot serve if he has a "fracture" in his foot or hand. It is a concrete physical rupture, something broken.
2. It extends to the destruction of a city or building, the collapse of walls or structures: in Jeremiah 6:1, a great "disaster" is seen coming from the north threatening Jerusalem, an image of the ruin that approaches.
3. The word also expresses a misfortune, a catastrophe that befalls a people or a person, the result of judgment: in Proverbs 16:18, "pride goes before ruin," meaning the downfall of one who is arrogant.
4. Applied to the suffering of body and soul, it designates the plagues and wounds inflicted by divine judgment: in Isaiah 30:26, God "will bandage the wounds of His people" like a bandage, an image of healing after the fracture.
5. Rarely, the word can mean the interpretation or hidden meaning of a vision or dream, what "breaks" or "shatters" the enigma.
H7667.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of breaking, shattering, fracturing. The cognate verb means "to break" or "to be broken." The image is that of a violent rupture, a break. It naturally expands from the physical (broken bone) to the political and moral (ruin of a city, collapse of a nation, destruction of a life).
H7667.emploi: The word appears 42 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Lamentations) and in Proverbs. In Leviticus and in the laws of purity, it describes the physical defects of the victims or the priest. In Proverbs, it designates the misfortune that follows pride and violence (Proverbs 15:4, 16:18, 18:12). The prophets use it extensively to announce the destruction of Jerusalem and enemy nations: Jeremiah uses it to describe the ravages of the Babylonian invasion, while Lamentations expresses the lament over the ruins of the city. In Isaiah, the word alternates between threats of destruction and promises of divine healing.
H7667.portee: This word reminds the believer that ruin and destruction are never accidental: they are the fruit of sin and rebellion against God. But it also teaches that God can heal wounds and restore: ruin does not have the final word. For those who suffer, this word helps to name the reality of suffering without denying it, while reminding that God remains the healer who can restore.

sens: Cultivated cereal, its grains intended for food
Supply of wheat bought or sold as a commodity
H7668.detail:
1. Wheat is the cultivated cereal that the peoples of the Middle East use as a staple food. It is a plant from which grains are harvested to be eaten or transformed into flour and bread. In the story of Joseph, Jacob sends his sons to buy wheat in Egypt (Genesis 42:1-2) because famine threatens Canaan and Egypt produces it in abundance.
2. The word also refers to the commodity itself, wheat as a traded good: it is bought, transported in sacks, and sold in the market. When Jacob's family brings back wheat from Egypt (Genesis 42:26), it is the harvest transformed into an economic good that can be loaded onto donkeys to be brought home (Genesis 43:2).
H7668.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁבֶר (she.ver) refers to the idea of breaking, of fracture: the grains of wheat, when crushed or harvested, separate from the ear. It is through this image of fragmentation that the language designates the wheat itself. The word belongs to a family that also evokes rupture and breakage, but here it has specialized to name this fundamental grain.
H7668.emploi: Wheat appears 9 times in the Old Testament, especially in the account of Joseph and the famine in Egypt (Genesis 42-44). It is the staple food that famine makes precious: Jacob sells his sons as slaves to buy it, and reserves are made. The word is also used to designate wheat as an object of trade and tax (Nehemiah 10:31) or as a good that unscrupulous merchants eagerly watch over in times of famine (Amos 8:5). In all cases, it is a vital commodity.
H7668.portee: Wheat reminds us that human life depends on God's providence and earthly crops. For the Christian, it is also the image of the grain of wheat that falls to the ground and dies to produce much fruit (John 12:24), which Jesus applies to his own sacrifice. Wheat symbolizes abundance and life, and its absence signifies misery and death.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Caleb
H7669.detail: Sheber is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Caleb and Maacah, Caleb's concubine. He appears only once in the Bible, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:48 in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. His name, which means "break" or "fracture," was borne by this member of the family of Hezron, whose descendants played an important role in the history of Israel.
H7669.origine: The name Sheber comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to break" or "to shatter." This image of rupture or fracture was common in Hebrew onomastics, where names often carried evocative meanings related to events or qualities.
H7669.emploi: Sheber is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:48, in the context of a genealogical list. He is identified as the son of Caleb and Maacah, his concubine. This mention is part of the genealogies of Judah, which establish the lineages of tribal leaders and their families. Sheber had several brothers and half-brothers, all listed to document Caleb's descent and tribal heritage in Israel.

sens: violent blow that injures or destroys
bone fracture or deep wound
calamity sent as divine punishment
H7670.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a violent blow that damages or destroys — an injury inflicted by force. In Jeremiah 17:18, the prophet asks God to strike his persecutors with a "double plague," meaning two great misfortunes that will overwhelm them.
2. It can also evoke a fracture or a wound that severely weakens the body. In Ezekiel 21:11, "broken loins" express the physical and moral pain of a person overwhelmed by suffering — an image of complete collapse.
3. By extension, the word designates a calamity, a plague that God sends to punish: not only a bodily injury but a misfortune that strikes a whole person or people.
H7670.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to break," "to shatter." It evokes the image of a solid thing fragmenting under a blow — hence the idea of violent destruction. The same root appears in other Hebrew words denoting rupture and fracture. This term belongs to the family of biblical vocabulary related to ruin and divine punishment.
H7670.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament, in contexts of suffering and divine judgment. In Jeremiah 17:18, it is a curse that the prophet calls down on his enemies — God must strike them with a double plague, meaning complete destruction. In Ezekiel 21:11, the expression "broken loins" describes the physical and emotional overwhelm of a person devastated by misfortune. In both cases, the word carries the idea of a violent and irreparable blow.
H7670.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of suffering and judgment. For the believer, it expresses that God is not indifferent to injustice: he can intervene to punish persecutors and defend the oppressed. It is a word of confidence in divine intervention, even if it remains formidable.

sens: Place in the Promised Land, point of retreat during the initial defeat against Ai
H7671.detail: Schebarim is a location near the city of Ai, in the Promised Land. During the first attempt to conquer Ai, the Israelites are routed by the inhabitants; they flee to Schebarim, where the pursuers strike them as they descend (Joshua 7:5). The name means "the breaches" or "the passages," which likely evokes an area of rugged terrain or narrow passages.
H7671.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁבָרִים (shevarim) comes from the root שׁבר (shavar), which means "to break" or "to shatter." In the plural, "the breaches" or "the ruptures" naturally designate passages or openings in the terrain. This geographical name reflects the topography of the place: a region of ridges and valleys through which the escape route passed.
H7671.emploi: Schebarim appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 7:5, at the moment when Joshua launches a first attack against Ai. This initial attempt fails due to the violation of God's command by Achan, who hid forbidden plunder. The men of Ai pursue the fleeing Israelites to this location and strike them during their retreat, sowing panic and discouragement in the Hebrew camp. This passage marks a critical moment: the defeat reveals the seriousness of Achan's hidden sin and sets the stage for the following narrative, when Joshua will discover the cause of the failure.
H7671.portee: This place of defeat reminds us that victory in the Promised Land does not depend solely on military strength, but on obedience to God. The retreat to Schebarim shows how the hidden sin of one man weakens the entire people and how God judges the failure to follow his commands. For the reader, it is a lesson on the importance of confession and communal purity before advancing in God's work.

sens: to be filled with trouble and confusion
to lose composure in the face of something unexpected or terrible
H7672.detail:
1. To be dismayed means to be seized with deep trouble, a confusion that paralyzes. The word evokes the state of someone who has just received terrible news and no longer knows where they stand: this is what the nobles of King Belshazzar experience when they see the mysterious writing appear on the wall (Daniel 5:9).
2. This trouble is accompanied by a loss of composure, an inability to react clearly. Dismay is not just a fleeting emotion: it paralyzes and disarms the one who feels it in the face of the incomprehensible.
H7672.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁבַשׁ (shebash) expresses the idea of confusion, deep trouble. Its etymology suggests a loss of clarity and mental firmness, a collapse of assurance and self-control. The word belongs to a family that evokes disorder and inner agitation.
H7672.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 5:9. The context is memorable: King Belshazzar organizes a great feast, profanes the vessels of the temple in Jerusalem, and at the height of his pride, sees a mysterious hand trace an inscription on the wall. In the face of this prodigy, the king's color changes and his nobles, his most powerful advisors, are dismayed: none of them can decipher the writing or interpret this divine sign. It is a moment of total rupture: human wisdom is annihilated before the direct intervention of God.
H7672.portee: This word teaches us that in the face of God's power, all human wisdom and confidence collapse. The great ones of this world, accustomed to commanding and controlling situations, discover that there exists a reality that infinitely surpasses them. Dismay thus becomes the symptom of an encounter with the absolutely other: it reminds us that only God possesses true wisdom and that the fear of God should temper our self-confidence.

sens: to stop an action or activity
to rest, interrupt one's work
to disappear, to extinguish
to put an end to something, to remove
to destroy, to annihilate
H7673A.detail:
1. To cease means to stop an ongoing action: one ceases to do something. For example, God "ceased" His work on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2) — He had finished creating.
2. To rest or cease work means to stop after a period of effort. On the seventh day, God "rested" from all His work (Genesis 2:2), thus establishing the rhythm of weekly rest.
3. To disappear or extinguish: something ceases to exist, it is no longer seen. The Lord will "remove" the fierce beasts from the land (Leviticus 26:6) — they will no longer be there.
4. To put an end to something, to remove: one causes the cessation of a situation or state. God would "cause to cease" the pride of the haughty (Isaiah 13:11) — He would put an end to their pride.
5. To destroy or annihilate: to completely cease, to reduce to nothing. The king of Babylon will come and "destroy" this land, he will "remove" the men and beasts from it (Jeremiah 36:29) — total annihilation.
H7673A.origine: The Hebrew root שׁבת (sha-vat) evokes the fundamental idea of stopping, putting an end. It is from this root that the word Shabbat (שׁבָּת), the day of rest, comes, the seventh day when all work ceases in memory of God's rest at creation. The word belongs to a family that runs throughout the Bible and expresses the rhythm of rest in Israelite life.
H7673A.emploi: This word appears about 65 times in the Old Testament, especially in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus), among the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), and in the Writings. It first designates the cessation of work or movement (Genesis 2:2, Exodus 16:30), then the extinction of a life or situation (Leviticus 26:6 for disappear), and finally the divine action that puts an end to things — judgment, destruction, annihilation (Isaiah 13:11, Jeremiah 36:29, Ezekiel 30:10). The word thus has a broad palette: from peaceful rest to destructive judgment.
H7673A.portee: This word reminds us that rest is not a weakness, but a divine command: God Himself rested, and He commands His people to cease work one day in seven. But it also shows us that only God has the power to put an end to injustices, malice, and the plans of the wicked — it is His sovereign prerogative. For the believer, it is both an invitation to confident rest and an assurance that the Lord controls history.

sens: To mark the seventh day by ceasing all work and dedicating oneself to rest
To let the land rest for an entire year according to divine law
To solemnly celebrate the rest prescribed by the Law
H7673B.detail:
1. To observe the Sabbath means to respect the divine order to cease all activity on the seventh day to rest and honor God. The word evokes the concrete action of "following," of "keeping" this sacred rest: in Leviticus 23:32, the Israelites are called to "celebrate" their Sabbath from the evening of the ninth day to the evening of the tenth, humbling themselves before God.
2. The land can also "observe the Sabbath" in the sense that it must remain at rest, without being cultivated, according to the cycle of years: in Leviticus 25:2, God prescribes that "the land shall rest" as a Sabbath in His honor, which shows that this observance extends to all of creation.
3. Celebrating the Sabbath also means rendering solemn worship to it, recognizing its holiness through an attitude of reverence and obedience towards God who established this day.
H7673B.origine: The verb שׁבַת (shavat) is directly related to the noun שַׁבָּת (shabbat, the Sabbath), which means "rest" or "cessation." The root expresses the fundamental idea of stopping, ceasing an activity. The verb thus designates the act of maintaining or keeping this rest, not as passivity, but as active obedience to divine will. It is an act of fidelity towards God and His commandment.
H7673B.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided texts, in the context of the Law of Leviticus. It expresses the action of the Israelites who "celebrate" the Sabbath of the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), and also the action of the land that "rests" according to the sabbatical cycle of seven years. These two uses show that the observance of the Sabbath concerns not only the people of Israel but also encompasses all of creation: humans must cease their work, and the land itself must know rest.
H7673B.portee: Understanding this verb invites the Christian to grasp the Sabbath, not as a mere prohibition against working, but as a positive act of trust in God and obedience to His will. It is to recognize that rest is not a luxury, but a spiritual and physical necessity that God Himself has inscribed in the rhythm of creation. Observing the Sabbath is to affirm that God provides for our needs and that our value is not based on our productivity.

sens: Stop of work, loss of time
Abstention, the act of refraining from doing something
Null result, outcome of nothing
H7674.detail:
1. The interruption of work: when one stops working, one loses the time and production that could have been achieved. In Exodus 21:19, if a man strikes another and injures him, the one who struck must compensate the injured for the lost time — the "interruption of work" — that is, to indemnify for the days he could not work due to the injury received.
2. Abstaining from something, refraining: it is the voluntary cessation of an action. Proverbs 20:3 encourages turning away from quarrels and disputes, not engaging in them. It is a mark of wisdom to "abstain" from conflicts rather than to throw oneself into them like a fool.
3. An action that leads to nothing, which remains barren: in Isaiah 30:7, the help of Egypt is called "a noise that leads to nothing," meaning wind, emptiness, something that disappears without producing any fruit or concrete result.
H7674.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of sitting, remaining still, ceasing. Its primary meaning is thus stopping, inactivity — that which remains without action or production. This root is close to other Hebrew words denoting rest or cessation of activity.
H7674.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, with nuances related to a stop or cessation. In Exodus 21:19, it concretely refers to the interruption of a wounded person's work, which is why he must be compensated. In Proverbs 20:3, it takes on a more voluntary and moral sense: to abstain from quarrels out of wisdom. In Isaiah 30:7, it expresses futility, nothingness — something that stops without ever leading to anything. The word thus oscillates between involuntary stop (the injury), voluntary stop (refraining), and absence of result (ending up with nothing).
H7674.portee: This word reminds the reader that every cessation has a cost: whether imposed by suffering or chosen, it weighs heavily. But it also emphasizes that sometimes, stopping — refusing a quarrel, for example — is the path of wisdom. And it warns against sterile efforts, those that produce nothing: better a voluntary stop than to persist in what leads to nothing.

sens: Furniture or place where one sits
Royal throne or place of honor
Dwelling, fixed establishment
Position, state of residence
Domination or authority
H7675.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: it is a piece of furniture intended to receive someone sitting, like the royal throne with its six steps described in 1 Kings 10:19, with its arms and lions on either side. It is simply the seat where one sits.

2. By extension, the seat becomes a symbol of power and honor: the king's throne, his prominent place. When speaking of the "seat" of the king, it refers not only to the object but also to the dignity and authority it represents.

3. The word also evokes a fixed establishment, a place where someone dwells or establishes themselves durably. The idea of a seat carries with it that of residence, a place where one has taken root.

4. In Lamentations 3:63, "sitting" simply refers to the physical position of those who mock the prophet — they are sitting near him.

5. When the text says "reign" in Amos 6:3, the word seat is understood as the seat of power, the domination itself: bringing near the reign (i.e., the seat) of violence means establishing violence in a position of authority.
H7675.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁבֶת comes from the root יָשַׁב (yashav), which means "to sit" or "to dwell." It is a noun formed from this root and retains the image of one who sits or resides somewhere. The same root gives the word שְׁבוּת (shibout, captivity), as captivity literally means "the state of one who sits" — that is, being stuck in one place against one's will.
H7675.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate a seat or a place. Two occurrences describe the king's throne (1 Kings 10:19 and 2 Chronicles 9:18), where the seat is the material object of royal power with all its ornaments. One occurrence in 2 Samuel 23:7 uses it in the sense of "place" or "location." In Lamentations 3:63, it refers to physical posture: "sitting." In Amos 6:3, the word takes on a nuance of "domination" or "reign." Finally, in Obadiah 1:3, sitting on high places refers to both the physical position and the feeling of an established and unshakeable power.
H7675.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the notion of power and stability. A royal seat is not just furniture: it is the center of command and judgment. For the believer, it reminds us that all earthly power — even as magnificent as King Solomon's throne — is fragile and fleeting, while the seat of the Lord remains eternal.

sens: The seventh day of the week, dedicated to rest and worship of God
Annual Day of Atonement, when the people repent
Year of rest every seven years, during which the land is left fallow
Period of seven days, the week
H7676.detail:
1. The sabbath is the seventh day of each week, established by God as a mandatory day of rest. In Exodus 20:8-10, God commands: "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy... the seventh day is a day of rest"; no work should be done on that day, nor should a burden be carried outside the city (Jeremiah 17:21-22). It is a sign of the covenant between God and His people (Exodus 31:13-16).

2. The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) is also called a sabbath because it is a solemn day of rest and atonement (Leviticus 16:31), when the people repent for their sins.

3. Every seven years, Israel observes a sabbatical year: the land itself rests, no cultivation is done, and the poor are allowed to eat what grows naturally (Leviticus 25:2-6). Leviticus 26:34 speaks of the land that "will enjoy its sabbaths" when its inhabitants are exiled — the land will finally rest.

4. The word can also refer to an entire week, a period of seven days (Leviticus 23:15-16 speaks of counting "seven sabbaths" = seven weeks).
H7676.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to cease, to stop." Shabbat literally denotes a stop, an interruption of work. In Hebrew, the verb shabat means "to stop, to cease." The sabbath is thus the day when work stops — just as God Himself rested on the seventh day after creation (Exodus 20:11). It is a day marked by the absence of productive activity and the consecration to God.
H7676.emploi: The sabbath is mentioned 89 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and among the prophets. God establishes it as an eternal commandment: Exodus 20:8-10 places it among the Ten Commandments. Prophets like Jeremiah (17:21-27) and Isaiah (56:2-6, 58:13) insist that the people keep it, for violating the sabbath is a serious infidelity. With the exile, the sabbath becomes a visible sign of attachment to the covenant (Leviticus 26:34; Ezekiel 20:12-20). The Law also enumerates the sabbatical years (every seven years) and the Jubilee (every 50 years), when debts are forgiven and slaves are freed. The notion of rest enriches: initially physical, it becomes spiritual — rest in God, trust, relinquishing human effort.
H7676.portee: The sabbath teaches the believer that he cannot do everything by his own effort. A day of rest each week reminds us that the world depends on God, not on our works. It is a lesson in humility and faith: to let grow, to let God act, to trust in His providence. For the modern reader, the sabbath invites reflection on how one "sanctifies" their rest — that is, how one dedicates it to God, to reflection, to relationship with Him and with family, rather than filling it with sterile busyness.

sens: Cessation of work observed on the seventh day of the week, dedicated to God
Day of atonement when the people rest and humble themselves before God
Sabbatical year when the land rests without being cultivated
Solemn feast days marked by cessation of work and a holy assembly
H7677.detail:
1. The sabbath rest is primarily the rest of the seventh day of the week, when all work ceases. It is a rest dedicated to the Lord, a holy day when no work should be done (Exodus 31:15: "the seventh day is the sabbath, the day of rest dedicated to the Lord"). This day marks the divine rhythm of creation: six days of work, followed by a complete day of rest.
2. The term also refers to the Day of Atonement, the day of atonements, when Israel observes a special rest by humbling themselves before God (Leviticus 16:31: "It shall be a sabbath for you, a day of rest, and you shall humble your souls"). It is a day of inner silence and repentance.
3. It can signify the sabbatical year, which occurs every seven years, when the land itself must rest without being plowed or sown (Leviticus 25:4: "the seventh year shall be a sabbath"). Even the land has a right to its rest.
4. The term also applies to solemn feast days such as the Feast of Trumpets or the first and last days of the Feast of Tabernacles, days marked by a holy convocation and the prohibition of servile work (Leviticus 23:24: "you shall have a day of rest, proclaimed with the sound of trumpets").
H7677.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁבָּתוֹן (shabbaton) comes from the root שׁבת (shabat), which means "to cease, to stop." The suffix -ōn indicates a characteristic or distinctive quality. This term is closely related to the word שַׁבָּת (shabbat, sabbath), which designates the day of rest itself. The root expresses the fundamental idea of interruption of work, a pause in activity, inscribed at the heart of the divine rhythm of creation.
H7677.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the Law, primarily in Leviticus and Exodus. It primarily designates the rest of the seventh day (Exodus 16:23, 31:15, 35:2), this holy day when all work ceases and the people dedicate themselves to God. It also applies to the Day of Atonement, a solemn sabbath when Israel humbles itself (Leviticus 16:31), as well as to solemn feasts like the Feast of Trumpets and the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:24, 23:32, 23:39). The word can finally designate the sabbatical year, when the land rests (Leviticus 25:4-5). In all these uses, it signifies a cessation of work or ordinary activity, marked by a holy dimension and often by a convened assembly.
H7677.portee: The sabbath rest teaches Israel a fundamental truth: work is not the essence of life, and man cannot be self-sufficient. This day reminds us that God is the master of time and that rest, far from being laziness, is an act of obedience and trust. For the believer, this principle reveals that our strength comes not from our constant efforts, but from our dependence on God, and that a righteous life balances action and rest, work and worship.

sens: Levite during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah
H7678G.detail: Shabbethaï is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Jerusalem. His name means "sabbath-like," that is, related to the sabbath. He appears in Ezra 10:15 among those who opposed the expulsion of the foreign women that the Israelites had married.
H7678G.origine: The name Shabbethaï comes from the Hebrew root שַׁבַת (shabat), which means "to rest" or "to cease," from which the word "sabbath" derives. The suffix -aï indicates a particular connection to this notion. It is a theophoric name typical of the time of the return from exile.
H7678G.emploi: Shabbethaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:15. At that time, Ezra undertakes a strict religious reform by asking the Jewish men of Israel to send away the foreign women they have married. Shabbethaï, as a Levite, plays a role in this controversy: he is among those who oppose Ezra's decision, calling for a more merciful approach toward these women and their children.

sens: Levite during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah
H7678H.detail: Schabbethaï is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during the public reading of the Law after the return from exile in Babylon. He is among the Levites who "explained the law to the people" (Nehemiah 8:7), meaning he helped make the sacred text understandable to the Israelites who returned to Jerusalem. His role was therefore to teach and clarify the Torah so that everyone could understand God's will.
H7678H.origine: The name Schabbethaï means "sabbath-like," derived from the Hebrew root שָׁבַת (shabat), which means "rest" and has given rise to the word "sabbath." This name recalls the day of rest dedicated to God in the Mosaic law. It likely reflects the importance of the sabbath in the religious life of Israel.
H7678H.emploi: Schabbethaï appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 8:7. He is presented as one of the Levites responsible for explaining the Law to the people during the great assembly in Jerusalem, after the return from exile. This moment is crucial: it is a renewal of the covenant between God and His people, and the Levites play the role of interpreters and spiritual teachers. Schabbethaï is named in a list of his colleagues, all engaged in this teaching work.

sens: Levite during the time of the restoration of the Temple after the Babylonian exile
H7678I.detail: Schabbethaï is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Jews return from exile and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. He is among the leaders of the Levites responsible for the external affairs of the house of God, that is, for the administration and maintenance of the Temple building (Nehemiah 11:16).
H7678I.origine: The name Schabbethaï means "sabbath-like," related to the rest of the sabbath: it comes from a Hebrew root evoking interruption and rest. It is a theophoric name, that is, carrying religious meaning, common among the Levites, men dedicated to worship and the observance of divine commandments.
H7678I.emploi: Schabbethaï is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 11:16. He appears in the list of the leaders of the Levites who participated in the restoration of Jerusalem after the return from exile, around the 5th century B.C. Alongside Jozabad, he was responsible for the external affairs of the Temple, an important role in the religious administration of the rebuilt community.

sens: Increase in number, power, or extent
Make great, give importance to
Praise, celebrate the works or qualities of someone
H7679.detail:
1. The word describes the action of giving increase, of magnitude: a nation grows in power and territory (Job 12:23 speaks of the increase that God gives to nations). It is a growth that makes something larger, more impressive.
2. It is also to make something or someone great by word: to magnify, exalt through the honor given. When Job says, "remember to exalt His works" (Job 36:24), he invites to proclaim the greatness of God's deeds.
3. The closest meaning in biblical usage is praise: to exalt means to recognize and celebrate the greatness, power, importance of someone, especially of God.
H7679.origine: The root שׂגא (sag) evokes the idea of growth and greatness. It belongs to the family of words that speak of increase and amplification. In Aramaic, the verb שְׂגָא (sega) has the same meaning. This Hebrew verb expresses the action of making great, either in quantity (to multiply) or in dignity (to honor).
H7679.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Job. In Job 12:23, God is the one who gives increase to nations, extending or reducing them according to His sovereign will: the meaning is that of increase in power and territory. In Job 36:24, it is an exhortation to exalt, to celebrate the works of God: the meaning shifts towards praise and recognition. In both cases, the context emphasizes divine majesty and sovereignty.
H7679.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that the greatness of peoples and works comes from God, and that our response must be praise. Exalting God is confessing that He is great, that He acts with power and wisdom. It is also to remember that our own spiritual growth depends on this recognition of His greatness.

sens: Become larger, more important, multiply
Be in abundance, in large quantity
Grow, gradually increase
H7680.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the action of growing or amplifying: something that increases in size or importance. In Ezra 4:22, the king fears that evil will "increase" if he does not exercise vigilance — it is the image of a threat that grows and spreads.
2. It also means to be present in large quantity, in abundance: a rich and generous reality. Nebuchadnezzar and King Darius wish that "peace" be given "with abundance" (Daniel 4:1 and 6:25) — a peace that is not measured by little, but that overflows, that manifests fully.
3. It is a movement of growth: the image of something that naturally increases, that multiplies and spreads, like a plant that grows or a population that develops.
H7680.origine: The word is an Aramaic form of the verb שׂגא (sa.ga in Hebrew, H7679), which expresses the fundamental idea of growing and amplifying. The root evokes a movement of expansion and increase. It is a word from biblical Aramaic, the language spoken in the Eastern kingdoms at the time of the captivity, used in certain passages of Daniel and Ezra.
H7680.emploi: The verb appears 3 times in the Aramaic books of the Bible. In Ezra 4:22, it refers to the growth of a problem: the "evil" that "increases" if one does not take heed. In the royal letters of Daniel (4:1 and 6:25), the pagan kings themselves invoke a peace that comes "with abundance" — the word takes on a shade of generosity and fullness. It is a term that the foreign sovereigns in the narrative use to bless the peoples, showing that even non-believers recognize the notion of abundant blessing.
H7680.portee: This word reminds us that everything grows — both good and evil. It invites the reader to vigilance: not to let bad influences amplify. It also shows that true divine blessing is not stingy, but abundant: God offers peace not drop by drop, but generously. It is a word of hope about the rich and overflowing nature of what God grants.

sens: father of Jonathan, one of David's warriors
H7681.detail: Shage is a character from the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is known as the father of Jonathan, referred to as "Jonathan, son of Shage" (1 Chronicles 11:34), who was one of the thirty valiant warriors in the service of King David. Jonathan is designated as coming from Harar, a region whose inhabitants, the Hararites, were among David's best soldiers.
H7681.origine: The name Shage literally means "one who wanders" or "the wanderer." It is a name that evokes the idea of straying from the path. It appears in the lists of David's warriors, recorded in the memory of Israel for his notable descendants who served the king.
H7681.emploi: Shage is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:34, where he is identified as the father of Jonathan the Hararite, one of David's thirty valiant warriors. He is also called Shagée in some textual traditions. His name appears solely to establish the genealogy of his son, who earned him a place in history as the parent of a renowned soldier.

sens: be high, inaccessible
be safe, protected
exalt, glorify
act with height, with strength
H7682.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of something that stands high, above reach: a fortress on a mountain that cannot be taken, a city "too strong" to be conquered (Deuteronomy 2:36). It is the idea of what is out of reach, lofty.
2. From this comes the meaning of protection and safety: if you are high, you are in a safe place. God "protects" those who trust in Him (Psalms 91:14), placing them out of danger as one elevates something high to shelter it.
3. For God Himself, the verb means "exalt," "glorify": His name alone is "elevated" (Psalms 148:13), above all creation. It is to recognize His absolute sovereignty.
4. Finally, the verb can mean "to act with height" or "to dominate": when God "raises" His enemies against a people (Isaiah 9:10), He establishes them in a position of strength and hostile superiority.
H7682.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂגַב comes from a root that expresses the idea of height and strength. It is related to the word שׂגֵב (sagév), "refuge," and to the word גֹּבַה (govaH), "height." The fundamental image is that of a raised place, dominating, inaccessible — a natural refuge. The verb retains this force: to be high is to be safe, to dominate.
H7682.emploi: The verb appears 20 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and in Isaiah. It is used in three main contexts: first to speak of fortresses or places "too strong" to be taken (Deuteronomy 2:36). Then to express the protection and safety that God offers to those who believe in Him: God "protects," "delivers" (Psalms 91:14, Proverbs 29:25). Finally, it describes the exaltation of God, His incomparable glory (Psalms 148:13, Isaiah 2:11), and sometimes His sovereign action that establishes someone in a position of domination. The word always emphasizes the idea of a position of strength or glory, whether physical, moral, or spiritual.
H7682.portee: This verb reminds the believer that God is the inaccessible height, the impregnable refuge. When one entrusts their life to God, they are "elevated" out of reach of evil: they find protection and safety not by their own strength, but by the Lord who places them in a safe place. It is also an invitation to glorify the name of God alone, to recognize that He is infinitely above all that exists.

sens: To go astray, to take the wrong path
To make a mistake, to commit a sin unknowingly
To be led astray, to deviate from the right way
H7683.detail:
1. To stray primarily means to physically or mentally misdirect oneself: to go sideways instead of going straight. Job 12:16 describes one who "strays or causes others to stray" as someone who loses their way or leads others off the right path.
2. Specifically, to stray means to commit a fault or sin out of ignorance or inadvertence, without malicious intent. Leviticus 5:18 speaks of the "fault he committed unknowingly": the Lord acknowledges that there is a difference between erring unintentionally and sinning willfully.
3. Spiritually, to stray means to deviate from obedience to God, at least temporarily. The psalmist confesses: "Before I was afflicted, I went astray" (Psalms 119:67), showing how divine correction brings one back to the right path.
H7683.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁגג (shagag) evokes the image of one who deviates, who strays. Its root expresses the idea of making a mistake or missing one's goal. The word belongs to the family of terms describing error or deviation: one who strays consciously or unconsciously leaves the straight path.
H7683.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Old Testament, mainly in the context of atonement sacrifices and moral life. Leviticus 5:18 and Numbers 15:28 place it within the legal and religious framework of forgiveness for faults committed unknowingly: the Law provides for a special sacrifice to restore communion when one has erred unintentionally. Job 12:16 uses it in the broader sense of diversion or seduction. Psalms 119:67 situates it in the personal experience of the faithful who recognizes their past straying and correction by the Lord. The word thus designates human error, which can be forgiven if it is not willful.
H7683.portee: This word teaches a fundamental truth of faith: God distinguishes between sin committed out of ignorance or inadvertence and deliberate sin. It shows us that being human means being able to err, and that divine correction aims to straighten us and bring us back to obedience. It also offers comfort: if we stray without malicious intent, the Lord provides a means of repair and restoration. It is an invitation to remain vigilant and to humbly accept discipline.

sens: Action committed without intention, by mistake or ignorance
Sin committed without wanting to, through forgetfulness or unconscious failure
Error or fault committed without realizing it
H7684.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes an action done without the intention of doing it, inadvertently or through lack of awareness. It is to act without realizing what one is doing, like a murderer who kills someone unintentionally and can seek refuge in a city of refuge (Numbers 35:11).
2. In the Law, unintentional sin is that which the believer commits unknowingly or unwillingly: he transgresses a commandment of the Lord, but his heart did not intend it (Leviticus 4:2). This is different from deliberate sin, committed with intent.
3. This type of fault calls for a reparative offering to obtain forgiveness, not condemnation. When the whole assembly sins unintentionally, it offers a young bull as a burnt offering (Numbers 15:24). The believer who sins alone unintentionally offers a goat (Numbers 15:27).
H7684.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to stray" or "to wander." It describes the state of one who has not seen, who has lacked awareness or attention. This is why it opposes voluntary sin, the sin of rebellion against God. In Greek, the Septuagint often translates it with a word meaning "without intention" or "without knowledge."
H7684.emploi: The word appears 18 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in Leviticus and Numbers, where it structures the entire law of atonement sacrifices. It distinguishes unintentional faults (which call for a sacrifice) from voluntary faults (which incur a more serious condemnation). It is also found in judicial matters: one who kills unintentionally (not a murderer) has the right to seek refuge in a city of refuge and live there safely (Numbers 35:11; Joshua 20:9). In Ecclesiastes, the word retains the sense of error, of clumsiness (Ecclesiastes 10:5).
H7684.portee: This word reminds us that God makes a distinction between our sins committed with intention and those that escape us through weakness or ignorance. It assures us that God knows our hearts: He does not condemn us for what we did not intend to do. At the same time, it invites us to awareness: even our unintentional sins require repair and purification. It is a grace that the Lord grants us ways to reconcile, even when we fail unintentionally.

sens: to grow, to develop (for a plant)
to increase in size or strength
H7685A.detail:
1. To grow, to develop: this verb describes the natural growth of a plant or vegetation. In Job 8:11, it is asked whether the rush can grow without marsh, or the reed without moisture — the image is that of a plant that grows, that gradually increases according to the favorable conditions given to it.
2. To increase in size or strength: the word can extend to the broader sense of an increase, a progression toward strength or maturity. It is the idea that something grows and becomes more significant over time.
H7685A.origine: The verb comes from a Semitic root that evokes the idea of visible and progressive growth. The image is that of an ascent, an elevation: a plant that grows upward, rising above the ground. The root is simple and concrete, rooted in the observation of nature.
H7685A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the book of Job. Bildad, Job's friend, uses it to pose a rhetorical question: can the rush and the reed grow without the essential conditions for their life (the marsh and moisture)? This unique occurrence underscores the concrete and figurative use of the word: the growth of a plant illustrates the impossibility of a reality without its natural foundations.
H7685A.portee: This word invites reflection on the conditions of growth — both physical and spiritual. Just as a plant cannot grow without water and fertile soil, a person cannot grow in faith and maturity unless rooted in the conditions that God has established. It is a humble reminder that all growth requires solid and stable foundations.

sens: Look attentively, fix one's gaze on something or someone
Examine intensely, scrutinize
Contemplate from a high position or afar
H7688.detail:
1. To look attentively means to fix one's gaze on something or someone with intention. It is to set one's eyes on an object or person to see it clearly. In Song of Solomon 2:9, the beloved "looks through the window": he casts his eyes toward the one he desires to see.
2. To examine intensely means to scrutinize, to seek to understand well what one is looking at. In Isaiah 14:16, "those who see you fix their gaze upon you": they do not turn their eyes away, they observe attentively to better grasp who you are.
3. To contemplate from a high position or afar expresses the idea of a view that overlooks. In Psalm 33:14, God "observes all the inhabitants of the earth" from "the place of His dwelling": He looks from above, encompassing all with His gaze.
H7688.origine: The Hebrew verb shaggach comes from a root that evokes the idea of looking intently, of fixing one's gaze on something. In Hebrew, verbs of vision often express more than a simple passive sight: "observe" carries within it the idea of voluntary attention, of intention. The form used here (Hiphil) reinforces this notion of directed action.
H7688.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalm 33:14, it describes God's omniscient gaze observing all humans from heaven. In Song of Solomon 2:9, it depicts the beloved looking through the window: a tender act filled with desire. In Isaiah 14:16, it shows those who observe the king of Babylon with astonishment, fixing an intense gaze upon him. In each case, "observe" implies not only seeing but also directing one's attention to what one is looking at.
H7688.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals that God is not a distant spectator: He observes, He looks, He pays attention to our lives. It is a word of comfort and warning: nothing escapes the gaze of the Creator. It also invites us to contemplate God with the same intensity, not to regard Him distractedly but to fix an attentive and loving gaze upon Him.

sens: Of large size or major importance
Surpassing common measure, considerable
Inspiring respect or admiration through power and majesty
H7689.detail:
1. The word simply designates what is large, imposing, or considerable in size or importance. In Job 36:26, it qualifies God Himself: "God is great, but His greatness is beyond our understanding" — meaning that God surpasses our ability to fully comprehend Him.
2. It carries the idea of power and superiority. In Job 37:23, God is called "Great in power": the word emphasizes that His greatness is not merely a matter of size or rank, but of real power and unquestionable authority over all things.
3. This word evokes majesty and an impressive character, something that inspires admiration and awe. When it is said of God that He is "great", it acknowledges His transcendent nature and incomparability.
H7689.origine: This word belongs to Aramaic, the language spoken by the Jews after the exile. It derives from a root meaning "to grow" or "to rise", hence the idea of something becoming great or surpassing in height and importance. The usual Hebrew word for "great" is "gadol", but in these passages from the book of Job, written in Aramaic, we find "saggiya" to express the same notion.
H7689.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Job (36:26 and 37:23). These two uses focus on a single idea: the greatness of God and His incomparability. In both cases, the context is a meditation on the limits of human knowledge in the face of God — we cannot reach His complete understanding, nor even His physical presence. The greatness in question is never that of a creature, but always that of God alone, who combines strength, justice, and sovereign right.
H7689.portee: Meditating on the greatness of God reminds the believer that God cannot be reduced to our human categories or logic. This frees from anxiety: since God is truly great, He masters what escapes us and can be entirely trusted. It is an invitation to humility and worship.

sens: Of considerable size, importance, or power
Which is numerous, abundant, in large quantity
Intense, violent, extreme in degree
Rich, magnificent, generous in gifts
