H7690.detail: 1. Great describes what has remarkable size or importance: the great king of Israel who once built the temple (Ezra 5:11) was a powerful and renowned sovereign. 2. Great also means numerous or abundant: the prophetic tree has abundant fruits and provides food for all (Daniel 4:12), its resources are vast. 3. The word can qualify the intensity of an emotion or act: the king became angry and was violently irritated (Daniel 2:12), showing an extreme reaction; Belshazzar was very frightened (Daniel 5:9), his fear was intense. 4. Great can also mean rich or magnificent: the king gave Daniel many and rich gifts (Daniel 2:48), sumptuous and considerable presents that marked his favor.
H7690.origine: The Hebrew word saggi comes from a root expressing the idea of growth, abundance, and unfolding. It is related to other Hebrew terms denoting greatness and power. This vocabulary is particularly present in the Aramaic texts of the Old Testament (books of Daniel and Ezra), where it describes both material and visible realities (size, quantity, wealth) and emotional or moral states (intensity, strength).
H7690.emploi: Saggi appears mainly in the later books of Ezra and Daniel (13 occurrences in total), texts written in Aramaic where this word plays a key role. It characterizes the realities of the world of powers: the great kings (Ezra 5:11), the great dreams (Daniel 2:31, 4:10, 4:21), the great prophetic beasts (Daniel 7:5, 7:7). It also describes the intense emotions of pagan kings in the face of divine mysteries: violent fear (Daniel 2:12, 5:9), extreme joy (Daniel 6:23). The word constantly emphasizes the magnitude of the events that God accomplishes or reveals to the nations.
H7690.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is above all human greatness and that His works surpass all that kings and empires can conceive. When the sovereigns of the world are seized with fear or joy before divine mysteries, it is because they sense a power that infinitely surpasses them. Earthly greatness — wealth, power, magnificence — counts for nothing in the face of the undeniable greatness of the God of heaven.

sens: Act of being misled or deviating from the right path
Involuntary error, mistake
Moral or religious deviation
H7691.detail:
1. Straying is primarily an error, a mistake — getting lost in direction or judgment, like someone who strays while walking. It is an unintentional fault, not a deliberate sin. In Psalms 19:13, the psalmist asks God to forgive him for the straying he is unaware of, that is, the errors of which he is not conscious.
2. The word also expresses the idea of deviating from the right path. In this sense, straying is less about foolishness and more about a kind of deviation — one strays because they have lost sight of the right direction.
3. When applied to religious and moral life, straying refers to unintentional faults, those arising from ignorance or human weakness, rather than deliberate rebellion against God.
H7691.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of losing oneself or deviating. It shares the same imagery as the verb "to stray" in French: walking without clearly seeing where one is going, deviating from one's path.
H7691.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Psalms 19:13. In this prayer context, the psalmist acknowledges his imperfection before God and distinguishes between two kinds of errors: those he knows and can repent of, and those that escape him, which only God can purify him from. Straying refers to the unintentional gap, at the limit of our consciousness — a flaw of sinful human nature, rather than an act of rebellion.
H7691.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian does not sin only by deliberate intention but also by ignorance and weakness. It invites humility before God: to recognize that we do not see everything within ourselves and to ask for His help to be purified from hidden straying. It is an invitation to transparency and trust in a God who knows and forgives what we do not see.

sens: Poem or song expressing a complaint, a lamentation
Title or inscription of a psalm
H7692G.detail:
1. A lamentation is a song that expresses deep pain, a complaint addressed to God. Psalm 7 bears this title and is related to it: David cries out to the Lord, expressing his distress in the face of accusations from Cush, a Benjamite. It is a cry from the heart, a poetic lament that intertwines personal suffering and an appeal for divine help.
2. This word appears as the title of a psalm, in the tradition of musical inscriptions of the psalms. It likely designates a literary genre or a musical form intended to express the distress of the singer.
H7692G.origine: The precise etymology of the Hebrew word shigaion remains uncertain. It may be related to the idea of straying, wandering, or groaning. In biblical Hebrew, several words with similar roots express complaint and lamentation. This term belongs to the vocabulary of psalm titles, which often indicated the context or type of poem to be sung in the temple.
H7692G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, at the beginning of Psalm 7. It is an inscription in the title of the psalm, accompanied by the name of David and the context: the song addressed to the Lord regarding Cush, a Benjamite. This unique placement and the absence of later uses suggest that it is a technical term from ancient psalmic vocabulary, likely intended for temple musicians to indicate the character or style of the song to be performed.
H7692G.portee: Psalm 7 bears this inscription to invite the one who prays to recognize that lamentation, the honest complaint addressed to God, is a legitimate mode of prayer. Even in distress and unjust accusation, the believer can express themselves sincerely before the Lord. This title reminds us that the Bible does not hide painful questions and cries from the heart, but integrates them into worship and relationship with God.

sens: Musical or literary term from the title of Psalm 7 and the song of Habakkuk
H7692H.detail: 1. This word appears only once in the Bible, at the beginning of the prophetic song of Habakkuk 3:1. Its exact meaning remains debated among scholars: some see it as a musical term (perhaps a style of song or the name of an instrument), while others consider it an indication related to the literary or poetic genre of the piece. The form of the word may suggest a repetition or a swinging (the echo of the sound "gai" in Hebrew), which could evoke a plaintive song or a lament. In the absence of explicit context, the word remains enigmatic, but it clearly appears in the title of the text, like other musical or poetic indications found at the beginning of certain psalms.
H7692H.origine: The Hebrew shigayon (singular) or shigionoth (plural) has an uncertain etymology. Some relate this word to a root meaning "to wander" or "to stray," which could refer to a melancholic or wandering style of song. Others think of it as a borrowing or a technical term from the Temple's musical vocabulary whose meaning has escaped us. The exact root and etymology remain open questions for Hebrew scholars.
H7692H.emploi: The word shigionoth appears only once in Habakkuk 3:1, at the beginning of the prophet's song. This title of the song places shigionoth in the same position as other indications found at the beginnings of psalms (like "Maskil," "Miktam," or "Neginoth"), which strongly suggests a musical indication or a style of composition. The context shows that Habakkuk 3 is a prophetic prayer-song where the prophet contemplates God's power and asks for His grace amid judgment, which gives the title a solemn and intense tone.
H7692H.portee: Shigionoth reminds us that the Bible is a living text, meant to be sung, liturgically proclaimed, and meditated upon. This enigmatic word invites us to recognize that some secrets of worship and praise in the Temple remain inaccessible to us, but that God hears every prayer and every cry from the heart, whether it bears a known name or remains mysterious.

sens: Wife of the king, companion of the sovereign
Woman adorned with royal dignity and authority at the throne
H7694.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the wife of the king, one who shares his throne and life. In Nehemiah 2:6, the queen is seated beside the king in his palace, occupying a place of honor at his side.
2. More broadly, it refers to a woman invested with royal dignity, often placed in a position of honor and prestige. In Psalm 45:10, the queen stands at the right hand of the king, adorned with the gold of Ophir, symbolizing her splendor and importance in the kingdom.
H7694.origine: The Hebrew word שֵׁגָל (shégal) comes from a root that evokes the idea of companionship and company. Its Aramaic equivalent carries the same meaning. In the Hebrew Bible, this term is infrequent, highlighting that the queen was not always a central figure in the biblical narrative, unlike the royal traditions of some neighboring peoples.
H7694.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament. In Nehemiah 2:6, it refers to the queen sitting beside the king in the context of the Persian court, showing the importance of the queen in royal protocols. In Psalm 45:10, it likely refers to a poetic celebration of an ideal or eschatological queen, adorned with glory and placed in a position of honor. The context varies: political and diplomatic in Nehemiah, poetic and glorifying in the Psalm.
H7694.portee: This word reminds us that in Psalm 45, a royal hymn, the queen occupies a place of honor beside the king. For the believer, this evokes the image of the people of God or the Church as an honored bride, associated with the glory of the divine King. It is a biblical image of dignity and covenant.

sens: Royal wife or concubine, companion of the monarch
Woman who shares the power and honor of the throne
H7695.detail:
1. This word refers to the wife or concubine of the king, one who lives in the royal palace and shares his intimate life. In Daniel 5:2-3, King Belshazzar summons his wives and concubines to drink from the sacred vessels of the temple in Jerusalem — they are his feast companions, distinguished from mere servants.
2. Beyond the marital bond, the word suggests a woman who participates in royal life and holds a high status: she is mentioned alongside the king himself as a court figure. In Daniel 5:23, she is listed among those who participated in the sacrilege, alongside the nobles of the kingdom.
H7695.origine: This Aramaic word (the language of Daniel 5) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "associate" or "companion." Its Hebrew equivalent (H7694) refers to the queen. The word evokes the image of a woman closely linked to the king through proximity and sharing of royal power.
H7695.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in Daniel 5 (verses 2, 3, and 23), in the account of King Belshazzar's sacrilegious feast. Each time, it designates the women of the royal court, mentioned alongside the concubines and next to the king himself, highlighting their high status and participation in palace affairs.
H7695.portee: This word reminds us that in the ancient Near East, the king's women were not only his wives but also public figures of the royal court. The text of Daniel shows that these women, although they enjoy honor and proximity to the supreme power of the world, are not exempt from divine judgment when that power rebels against God.

sens: Loss of reason, disorder of the mind
Extravagant behavior or words that indicate a troubled spirit
In the prophets, access of divine inspiration perceived by unbelievers as madness
H7696.detail:
1. Madness is the loss of reason, the inability to think and act normally. David feigns this condition before King Achish: he "loses his mind" (1 Samuel 21:14), and the king drives him away, saying that he does not lack "madmen" in his entourage without needing to welcome more (1 Samuel 21:15).
2. Delirium manifests itself through acts or words that reveal a disturbed mind. When Jehu comes out after his anointing as king, people ask why this "madman" comes to him (2 Kings 9:11): they judge his behavior as senseless. Similarly, someone who "claims to be a prophet" can be locked up as mad if their behavior seems unreasonable (Jeremiah 29:26).
3. Among true prophets, this apparent madness hides genuine inspiration: when Israel mocks its prophets by saying, "The prophet is mad, the inspired man is in a frenzy" (Hosea 9:7), it is because the unbelieving people do not recognize God's voice in their passionate and vehement words.
H7696.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁגַע (shagah) expresses mental disorder at its root. It literally describes the shift from order to confusion, from clarity to mental disturbance. The Bible uses it to describe both true madness (illness, punishment) and intense prophetic behavior, which contemporaries judged incomprehensible.
H7696.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the passive form ("to be mad") or participial form ("the madman"). It first describes concrete cases: David simulates madness to escape the king of Israel (1 Samuel 21), Jehu's servants see the young prophet's behavior as that of a madman (2 Kings 9). It can also refer to a false prophet or someone suspected of being one (Jeremiah 29, Hosea 9). The important nuance appears in Hosea 9:7: the word "mad" applied to the true prophet shows that divine inspiration, with its vehemence and urgency, can resemble madness in the eyes of the unbelieving world that does not understand God's ways.
H7696.portee: This word reminds us that the world often judges faith and prophetic words as a kind of irrationality. The Christian who fully surrenders to God may seem foolish to those who only know human logic. It is also a warning: true prophecy must be discerned carefully, as the pretext of inspiration can mask true madness. Ultimately, this word invites us not to judge too quickly those whose zeal or dedication confounds us.

sens: Mental disturbance that removes reason and judgment
Disordered and uncontrolled behavior
State of confusion and disorientation of the mind
H7697.detail:
1. Delirium is a serious mental disturbance that deprives a person of reason and lucidity. It is a mental illness that renders someone incapable of clear thinking and controlling their actions. In Deuteronomy 28:28, God threatens to strike Israel with "delirium," meaning to make them mad and disoriented, alongside blindness and wandering.

2. Delirium manifests itself through chaotic, illogical behavior, such as that of Jehu who "drives in a mad manner" (2 Kings 9:20): he rushes forward without thinking, with a delirious impetuosity that alarms the watchmen.

3. It is also a state of dizziness and mental confusion that strikes the enemies of Israel. In Zechariah 12:4, God strikes those who ride the horses with "delirium," rendering them bewildered and unable to fight effectively.
H7697.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to make noise" or "to agitate," evoking the chaotic and noisy agitation of a troubled mind. This delirium is not mere dizziness: it is profound madness, a disturbance that completely disorganizes the person. The word carries the image of a being shaken, upset, deprived of sense.
H7697.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a state of madness or mental confusion sent by God as punishment or divine intervention. In Deuteronomy 28:28, it is part of the curses pronounced on the unfaithful people: God will strike them with diseases and mental disturbances. In 2 Kings 9:20, it characterizes Jehu's reckless and senseless conduct as he gallops without restraint. In Zechariah 12:4, God promises to strike the enemies of Israel with mental confusion to unsettle them in battle. In all cases, delirium is presented as a serious misfortune or as a divine weapon.
H7697.portee: This word reminds us that God controls even the minds of men and that a life without God, without wisdom and obedience, exposes one to madness and self-destruction. Unfaithfulness and rebellion against God lead to irrationality. For the believer, it is a call to seek clarity of mind and wisdom that comes from God alone.

sens: The young born of an animal, especially livestock
The progeny, what is born and reproduces in domesticated animals
H7698.detail:
1. The word refers to the young animals born together from a mother, particularly the young of livestock (cows, sheep, goats). It is equivalent to the English term "offspring": a goat that gives birth to a litter of kids, a ewe a litter of lambs. Deuteronomy 7:13 lists among the blessings that God promises "the offspring of your large and small livestock".
2. More broadly, the term refers to anything that is born, the reproductive capacity of livestock and its descendants, as a wealth that increases. The divine blessing pertains to this multiplication: "The fruit of your womb, […] the offspring of your large and small livestock, all these things will be blessed" (Deuteronomy 28:4). The opposite curse threatens the offspring: "it will leave you neither grain, nor wine, nor oil, nor offspring of your large and small livestock" (Deuteronomy 28:51).
H7698.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁ֫גֶר (shéger) comes from a root that expresses the idea of what grows, what is born and reproduces. It is used exclusively for animals, never for humans: it is a term from pastoral and agricultural vocabulary. The Bible uses it in the context of livestock and the wealth it represents.
H7698.emploi: The word appears five times in the Bible, only in Deuteronomy and Exodus, in contexts of divine blessing and curse. In Deuteronomy 7:13, God promises to multiply the offspring of livestock as a sign of His favor toward Israel. In Deuteronomy 28:4 and 28:18, the offspring figures among the covenant blessings or curses: it illustrates the prosperity or material ruin that obedience or disobedience to God brings. In Deuteronomy 28:51, it is precisely the deprivation of offspring that symbolizes the total dispossession of the people by the enemy. The term remains concrete and economic: it measures wealth and survival.
H7698.portee: This word reminds us that for Israel, divine blessing is expressed in concrete realities: land, harvests, and the multiplication of livestock. It shows how Deuteronomy links obedience to God with material and familial prosperity. It is a call to see God's hand in the abundance of daily life, and to understand that rejecting God leads to barrenness and loss.

sens: A woman's chest, particularly the breasts
A breast of an animal
Space between the breasts, intimate physical proximity
Breastfeeding and infant
Place of maternal tenderness
Object of beauty and desire
H7699A.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a woman's breasts, this part of the female body. In the Song of Solomon, the beloved admires her "breasts" (Song of Solomon 7:8); elsewhere they are compared to clusters of grapes or young deer (Song of Solomon 4:5), images of beauty and form. 2. The word also applies to animals: the udder, the gland that produces milk to nourish the young. Job wishes he had never been nursed (Job 3:12), a term that also encompasses the animal. 3. The breast is also this intimate space, where someone rests against the chest of the beloved. "Between my breasts" (Song of Solomon 1:13) expresses closeness, rest, carnal intimacy. 4. The word evokes breastfeeding: giving the breast to the infant, nourishing with one's milk. Isaiah speaks of weaning from the breast (Isaiah 28:9), meaning to cease breastfeeding when the child grows. 5. The maternal breast becomes a symbol of the tender relationship between mother and child, which has carried and nourished them since birth. Jacob blesses Manasseh with blessings from the breast (Genesis 49:25). 6. In the Song of Solomon, the breast is also celebrated as erotic beauty, an object of desire and pleasure, as reflected in the poetic admiration of the beloved for the body of his beloved.
H7699A.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁד (shad) comes from a root simply designating this part of the body. There is a variant שֹׁד (shod), very close. The word is used in biblical Hebrew in a direct and concrete manner, without detour. In Greek, the New Testament will use μαστός (mastos) for the same concept; in English, "breast" covers both the general idea of chest and the more specific sense of mammary glands.
H7699A.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poems and prophecies. The Song of Solomon contains the largest number (at least 8 occurrences), as it celebrates the beloved's body and the carnal intimacy between spouses: the poet magnifies the breasts of the beloved with images of beauty. The prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel use it to describe the growth of the young girl, or conversely to evoke mourning (striking the breast as a sign of sorrow) and the moral degradation of women who prostitute themselves. Job uses it when speaking of breastfeeding. The Psalms and Hosea associate it with the image of the nursing infant. The meaning thus varies: from admired beauty to the symbol of breastfeeding and maternal protection, passing through images of mourning or shame.
H7699A.portee: This word shows us that the Bible does not shy away from the human body or its beauty, particularly in the Song of Solomon: physical desire between spouses is celebrated as good and beautiful. It also reminds us that maternal tenderness, breastfeeding, and the protection of the child are strong biblical images of God's love. Finally, the contrast between the breast as a source of life and nourishment, and the breast that one strikes in mourning, shows us the depth of human emotions that the Bible recognizes and expresses.

sens: Breast or teat of a woman or an animal
Source of nourishing milk
Image of consolation and divine abundance
H7699B.detail:
1. The udder is the breast or chest, particularly of a nursing woman or an animal that feeds its young. Job 24:9 speaks of it in the literal sense: the orphan is torn from the udder of his mother, meaning he is separated from the milk and maternal care when he needs it most.
2. The udder is the source of milk that nourishes and sustains. This milk is concrete and vital: without it, the newborn dies. In Isaiah 60:16 and 66:11, the image becomes figurative but retains all its strength: the people of God must "suck the milk" of divine consolation and be "nourished and satisfied," just as a child at the breast receives life and comfort.
3. Motherhood, tender and generous consolation: this word evokes not only physical breastfeeding but also the loving relationship between mother and child, and by extension, the tenderness with which God comforts His people by spiritually nourishing them.
H7699B.origine: The Hebrew word שֹׁד (shod) literally means the udder or breast. It comes from the root that designates what covers or protects, since the udder is the center of protection and nourishment for the child. The word is used in the Old Testament to describe both the physical organ and, by poetic extension, everything that nourishes and consoles.
H7699B.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of tenderness or spoliation. In Job 24:9, it refers to the tragic separation of the orphan from maternal milk, illustrating the injustice faced by the poor. In the two uses in the book of Isaiah (60:16 and 66:11), the term shifts to the figurative: Jerusalem, or the faithful people, will be nourished by the abundant milk of divine consolations, like a child satisfied at his mother's breast. This image of nourishment and abundance emphasizes God's limitless generosity toward His people.
H7699B.portee: For the believer, the udder evokes the tenderness and reliability of divine care. While Job 24:9 recalls the cruelty of depriving the orphan, Isaiah 60:16 and 66:11 promise that God Himself will nourish His people with overflowing generosity, like a mother with her child. This biblical image speaks to the heart: it teaches that God is not distant, but close, a provider, attentive to our deepest needs.
